item.title: A Toolkit for a Liberated Art World - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“Radical politics,” “marginalized communities,” “feminist art” … If you see these terms peppering wall labels at a major museum, there’s an excellent chance the institution behaves in direct opposition to those values and groups. Scholars Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon, who were also among the organizers of the historic Strike MoMA protests in 2021, know this pattern all too well. It’s part of the neoliberal capture of art institutions, which Italian curator and activist Marco Baravalle lays bare in his new book, The Battleground of Art. Read on for a review by Husain and Dhillon, who write that it’s a toolkit for building a better, freer art world.

Meanwhile, in the United States, that art world finds itself at a crucial turning point. In the wake of the midterm elections, longtime nonprofit arts leader Jasmine Wahi reminds us that the fight is only beginning. She opines today about the importance of holding Democratic officials accountable not just for redressing the damage inflicted by the Trump administration, but also for taking its responsibility to artists and culture workers seriously. “Rebuilding the same inadequate baseline is not enough,” she explains.

More in the news today, including public backlash against Egypt’s arrest of the editor of an independent publication and San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato’s resistance against Silicon Valley and enshittifcation through his quietly subversive art. Heaven knows we could all use more of that.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins

In the afterglow of the blue-nami, those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition. | Jasmine Wahi

item.title: How Does an Artist Know When She’s Done? A Major Marisa Merz Retrospective Turns the Question on Its Head - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Italian artist Marisa Merz (1926–2019) was famously camera-shy. In rare snapshots, such as a captivating photograph taken by Claudio Abate at her 1975 solo show in Rome, she would retreat from the camera’s gaze. Before Abate’s camera, Merz appears clad in her woven nylon Scarpette (Little Shoes), 1968, her back to him as she gazes out an open window at the moon.

The turn away is emblematic of Merz’s artistic ethos writ large. As she once wrote, in a 1975 issue of Data Arte magazine, “The artist is already an established role, like the wife, the son. But I don’t go along with these roles.”

Merz was the only woman affiliated with Arte Povera, a loose movement christened in 1967 by curator Germano Celant that rejected the commodification of art and celebrated presence and materiality through nontraditional media and process-based practices. Even within this iconoclast milieu, she remained an outlier, not only for her inscription of domestic labor into her work—in her 1967 film The Count, she is seen in her kitchen sorting beans—but also for her use of figuration from the 1970s onward. Her unruly aluminum installations, paraffin pools, and woven forms were overlooked in the 1960s and 1970s, but she has gained wider recognition in recent years. Since the 1990s, major exhibitions of her work have been staged across Europe and the US, and in 2013, the Venice Biennale honored her with a Golden Lion.

Still, Merz remains evasive even as she enters the spotlight. A sprawling and polyphonic retrospective titled “Marisa Merz: La danza delle ore (The Dance of the Hours)” has taken over three Turin institutions on the centenary of her birth. Yet despite its exhaustive review of more than five decades of her work, she remains enigmatic. The Galleria d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea Torino (GAM) emphasizes her superposition of studio and home; the Fondazione Merz focuses on her material experiments; and the Castello di Rivoli explores her metaphysical engagement with space. All the while, Merz’s elusive central themes—transparency, metamorphosis, and alchemy—recur throughout.

True to the retrospective’s title, the suite of exhibitions doesn’t follow a chronological itinerary, if only because to do so is nearly impossible. Her biography remains shrouded in mystery. These are the known facts of her life before 1960: Born in Turin to a father employed by Fiat, she studied dance and later modeled in other artists’ studios. Even after garnering critical attention, she rarely titled or dated her compositions and struggled to lay them to rest. The title of her first and best-known installation, The Living Sculpture (1966), says it all, encoding her belief that completion is concomitant to a kind of death.

This unsettled attitude manifests in a provisional quality that prevails across the works on view. The Living Sculpture is a tentacular, sewn-aluminum work that originally dangled claustrophobically from the ceilings of her home and now hangs in glittering fragments at GAM and Castello di Rivoli. Her series of knobby clay “Testine (Little Heads),” made from the 1970s to the 2010s, are unfired and sometimes retain the rough corners with which they were cut in bricklike masses from a larger block of clay. Her abstracted faces, painted and drawn on paper, wood, and alabaster, are warped and blurred as if in motion; one untitled and undated graphite physiognomy rearranges itself in whirling lines of vortex-like eyes.

Merz, like her Arte Povera peers, was frustrated by fixity and drawn to materials that morph across time. Perhaps appropriately, the curators have displayed works that may be unfinished and come straight from the studio; whether she planned to continue them will never be known. Notes on hotel stationery and Post-its remain tacked, taped, and clipped directly onto her drawings and paintings, variably describing the emotions she hoped to capture (for example, “expressive and polished”), quoting from literature (one composition glosses Hölderlin’s final poem), or simply logging dimensions. There is a sense that Merz might yet return with needle, pencil, or brush and pick up where she left off.

As if to show how an idea remains unfixed, persisting and evolving as later generations take it on, the exhibitions stage encounters between Merz and contemporary women artists—including Leonor Antunes, Thea Djordjadze, and Miriam Cahn—whose work shares affinities with hers. Tacita Dean was commissioned to produce a body of film and photographs in Merz’s home and studio. The results include a 16 mm film diptych Via Milano 13 (2026) capturing scenes from Merz’s apartment near Turin’s Porta Palazzo market. In slow frames, we see a honeycombed assemblage of cardboard cylinders from rolls of toilet paper and paper towels; a chorus of “Testine” arranged on the spiraling table in her husband’s old studio; a painted, blue-haired visage with livid red lips fastened on a wall, its double mirrored upside-down in a glass surface below. Hung in constellated installations at GAM and Fondazione Merz, a complementary series of photographs likewise opens Merz’s private world to our curious eyes, often capturing works in situ among furniture and family photographs before their displacement to the exhibitions’ airy galleries. The film and images verge on invasion, contravening Merz’s injunction against photographic capture—except, of course, for the fact of the artist’s absence, palpable in Dean’s meditative, static shots.

Leaving this suite of exhibitions, I find Merz’s practice is even more fugitive than before. I am not the first critic to encounter this difficulty. Writing on her work for Artforum in 1992, Celant reflected, “The instant it is defined, it flees.” Like the artist herself, Merz’s works are chimerical, morphing with the shifting light, blurring at the edges of the frame, slipping out of sight.

item.title: Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic, urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue.

“MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Batista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon.

“Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Batista continues.

The letter makes reference to three sexual assault and misconduct accusations brought forth against the billionaire, all of which Black denies. One of the lawsuits was discontinued by the plaintiff, and an earlier lawsuit was dismissed by the court. A third lawsuit was allowed to move forward after a judge imposed a sanction. UltraViolet said it has not received a response from Spielberg's representatives.

Black left his role as CEO of his private equity firm Apollo Global Management in 2021, when news broke that he paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein’s first conviction for soliciting sex from a minor. Even though he stepped down as MoMA board chairman that same year, after Hyperallergic published an open letter signed by over 150 artists calling for his removal, Black remains a MoMA board trustee.

Public scrutiny of Black intensified in September, after the US House of Representatives unanimously approved a resolution to hold the MoMA trustee in contempt of Congress for defying subpoenas in an Epstein investigation. This month, Black sued California Representative Robert Garcia for defamation over public comments such as "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”

Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner, who initially posted an open letter to Spielberg on her Instagram, said she was “amazed” by the public response.

“Steven Spielberg has made his career making stories about the dignity of women and children,” Gardner told Hyperallergic at tonight's protest. “It's totally disgusting that he's accepting an award [at the film center named after Leon Black], who's currently in contempt of Congress for not producing NDAs and his involvement in the Epstein files.”

Last month, Gardner co-performed a staged reading of former Barclays CEO and JP Morgan executive Jes Staley's deposition on Epstein to the United States House Oversight Committee in July.

At this evening's protest, others carried signs pointing to Black's connections to pro-Israel and Zionist organizations. Black has reportedly donated money to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which denies that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and Birthright Israel, which is accused of serving as a propaganda campaign for the Israeli government.

“I can personally say I'm Jewish and it's specifically because of my Jewish values that we're here. Never again means never again for anyone,” one demonstrator, Janet Goodman-Clarke, told Hyperallergic. “Leon Black not only is a Zionist, but he's also named ad nauseam in the Epstein files.”

MoMA has not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment.

Artists, activists, and Epstein survivors have repeatedly gathered in front of MoMA demanding his ousting. Among those in attendance at today's action was Katie Fuller, arts educator and founder of the Time and Memory Project, who staged a separate protest calling for Black's removal in front of the museum with her sister in September.

Last month, Fuller teamed up with Epstein survivors, UltraViolet, and the Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts, to illustrate the extent of Epstein's network. The free, mobile installation displayed a timeline of President Donald Trump’s relationship with Epstein and contains thousands of books' worth of the released so-called “Epstein Files,” in which Black was mentioned over 8,500 times.

That protest included Dani Bensky, a dancer, educator, and Epstein survivor from 2004 to 2005. A few weeks after the action, Bensky wrote an op-ed for Hyperallergic condemning Black’s board position as “one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.”

Besides his investments in MoMA, Black has held enormous sway in the art world. In a newly released book by William D. Cohan, Black disclosed plans to convert the Woolworth Mansion into a tax-beneficial art foundation, which is expected to house works from his estimated $5 billion art collection, an asset that Epstein helped leverage as bank collateral.

Gardner said she had one simple message for the attendees of tonight’s benefit gala: “If you know, you're human garbage. And if you didn't know, you can't say that after tonight, because we're out here saying hi to everybody with our signs.”

item.title: Artnet’s Kalshi Partnership Faces Swift Backlash Online, But Advisers Are More Mixed - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The art world, as much as we love it, has never been accused of lacking opportunities for speculation. But apparently “there’s room for one more, honey.“

On Wednesday, Artnet announced that it had partnered with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that lets users bet on everything from election results to sporting events. Artnet will become Kalshi’s official art partner, helping select markets and supplying the auction data used to determine which bets pay out.

The reaction on Instagram was swift and, let’s say, not particularly kind.

“How convenient. Now you can misunderstand art from anywhere,” wrote one commenter.

“Listen y’all there simply weren’t enough ways to artificially inflate an artist’s market and destroy their career before they turn 30,” wrote another.

Then came perhaps the most inspired comment, which may be a prediction of Artnet’s next move on the chessboard: “UFC x ARTNET! ARTNET JOE ROGAN.”

The partnership comes seven months after Artnet, the auction-data and media company, announced a mergerwith the online art brokerage Artsy. The combined company is led by chairman Andrew Wolff, CEO of Beowolff Capital, which acquired majority stakes in both companies over the past year.

It also comes just days before New York’s marquee November sales, which will offer plenty of chances to put the partnership to the test. Kalshi introduced art-related prediction markets in May and already offers contracts on individual paintings, entire collections, and whether artists will break their auction records.

Take Yoshitomo Nara’s Candy Blue Night (2001), which is headed to Sotheby’s on November 16. Users can trade contracts on whether the painting will sell for more than $6 million or $7 million. They can also trade on major works by Francis Bacon, Andy Warhol, and Roy Lichtenstein that are coming up for sale.

For now, the money changing hands in Kalshi’s art markets is dwarfed by the value of the objects being bet on. On Thursday, a market for Sotheby’s Blaquier-Arrieta Collection showed a roughly 52 percent probability that the sale would exceed $500 million. At the time, it had attracted just $372 in trading volume.

Still, the idea of making money from an auction without having to buy anything has its attractions.

Wendy Cromwell, founder of the advisory firm Cromwell Art and a former Sotheby’s contemporary-art specialist, saw some promise in the idea but also reasons for concern.

“I do think it’s a way for people to participate in the community,” she said. She added that she meant people who are engaged with the art world, follow artists, and understand their markets, even if they aren’t collectors themselves.

But Cromwell also saw a potential problem: the advantage held by people with access to information the public doesn’t have.

“It’s going to be extraordinarily tempting for everybody because everyone in the art world has inside knowledge,” she said.

Philip Hoffman, founder and chairman of the Fine Art Group, was less enthusiastic. “I can’t see that it’s a great use to collectors,” he said. In his view, there’s no reliable way to predict the prices of major works, where personal preference, provenance, condition, and the whims of the wealthy can render even the most carefully considered valuations irrelevant.

Results for more ordinary works, he said, can be relatively predictable. The top of the market is another matter. “People get carried away if they truly want it, and there’s no price,” he said.

Hoffman recalled once guaranteeing a Willem de Kooning painting that everyone expected to fetch substantially more than $10 million. Then the stock market fell, bidders disappeared, and he was left owning the painting himself. He eventually sold it for $9.7 million, taking a $300,000 loss. In other words, even knowing who intends to bid is no guarantee of knowing what will happen when the auctioneer raises the gavel.

There are also more troubling possibilities.

The art market runs on information that isn’t always available to the public. Auction-house specialists usually know how many bidders are registered for a sale. Dealers and advisors may know who is interested in a painting, how badly they want it, and what they’re prepared to pay. Guarantors may already have a financial stake in a work before it reaches the auction block.

That’s an obvious problem for a prediction market. A casual participant might have access to auction estimates, past sales results, and whatever enthusiasm is circulating on social media. Someone closer to the sale, meanwhile, might know about confidential expressions of interest, guarantees, or the number of absentee bidders. The two would hardly be working with the same information.

Then again, access to sensitive information isn’t limited to senior specialists. Junior employees who help keep the wheels of commerce turning could also be privy to confidential bidding information, giving them an advantage over ordinary traders.

When Kalshi first moved into the art market in May, Christie’s and Phillips told ARTnews that they have robust policies governing the use of confidential information and participation in activities that present a conflict of interest. Both said those policies cover prediction markets. Sotheby’s declined to comment at the time.

For its part, Kalshi prohibits trading on material nonpublic information. Its rules for artwork-price contracts also bar certain insiders from participating, including consignors, bidders, guarantors, and auction-house employees involved in a sale. But identifying those people and enforcing those restrictions in a business built on discretion is a challenge of its own.

The question I can’t stop turning over: Could prediction markets influence the auctions themselves? One can imagine a feedback loop in which speculative enthusiasm on prediction markets drives expectations higher and sways real buyers. A collector who sees overwhelming confidence that a picture will blow past its estimate might begin to second-guess an advisor’s valuation. Dealers or other interested parties might also see an opening to stoke enthusiasm for an artist’s market.

There’s another intriguing possibility. Might collectors use prediction contracts to offset some of their auction spending, effectively hedging their exposure to a purchase? Or might they look for gaps between the expectations reflected on Kalshi and what they believe artworks will actually bring at auction?

But there’s a catch. Kalshi’s rules prohibit people who can influence an auction’s outcome from betting on it. And with so little money being wagered so far, there isn’t much to be made anyway.

For now, the gap between multimillion-dollar auctions and prediction markets with little real money on the line suggests that Kalshi’s art offerings are more experiment than alternative financial market.

Still, Artnet’s involvement adds another dimension. The company will help identify subjects for prediction markets and provide data from its Price Database to verify the outcomes. Kalshi will continue to design the contracts and operate the exchange. Artnet has said its newsroom will not be involved in creating the markets or verifying results.

For Cromwell, the important question is whether anyone should treat these predictions as a serious measure of what art is worth.

“I think it’s a fool’s game to listen to prediction markets,” she said. “If you’re spending lots and lots of money, you should do your own research and have your own convictions about what you want to spend.”

item.title: How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture - Hyperallergic
item.description:
We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures, when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition. The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.

Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.

Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice, rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.

item.title: How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint - Colossal
item.description:
Looking at the serene paintings that emerge from Sky Glabush’ s studio, it’s easy to feel a soft breeze sliding off bare summer shoulders or hear the crunch of leaves underfoot, their parched fibers reverberating across the autumn landscape. Transportive and atmospherically charged, the landscapes harness the allure of texture to draw the viewer in and invite them to stay a while.

Raised on the west coast of British Columbia and currently based in rural Ontario, Glabush has long been attuned to the natural world. He often identifies the feelings he associates with a particular place and translates that through color and intuitive interpretations of the terrain: the spindly, strangely straight tree trunks of a forest, for example, or the ways a sunflower echoes the radial form of the sun.

Glabush typically utilizes limited palettes that adhere to just one or two color families. He also mixes oil paint with granular particles, sand being the most common, although he’s used crushed quartz and raw pigment. Originally, the idea of combining materials emerged because the artist wanted, he says, to “obliterate the image… But I realized it didn’t destroy the image. It was still present and humming under that surface layer. So it gave me the freedom of deciding what I wanted to hold on to or what I wanted to erase.”

Adding and removing has since become integral to Glabush’s practice, which involves adding thin stains of paint and turpentine to the point of the painting becoming relief-like. He tends to begin with an architectural structure that anchors the work. Sometimes a grid and others a radial arrangement, the foundational patterns inform each resulting layer. Color, though, is always “the unifying principle, it is the energy and dynamism, it is the element of surprise. Each painting often goes through several iterations of colour before deciding on a direction.” 

Although he’s worked with other materials in the past and has particularly enjoyed carving, the conventions and limitations of painting always drew him back. “That period of experimentation with sculpture allowed me to treat my paintings in a more physically robust and experimental way. But even during my most experimental period, I saw myself as a painter and wanted to find a way to express myself within that language,” he tells Colossal.

Some of the works here will be on view in Glabush’s solo exhibition, If the Wild Bird Could Speak, on view from November 20 to January 9 at Alison Jacques in London. Until then, explore more of his paintings on Instagram.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article How Sky Glabush Conjures Atmospheric Landscapes in Sand and Oil Paint appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: MoMA Shells Out $200,000 for Inaugural Ambasz Prize for ‘Nature-Reconciled’ Architecture, Half of Which Will Go To Plant Trees - ARTnews.com
item.description:
As experts gather in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations COP31 climate change conference, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker is warning of devastating warming by 2100, and the EU reports that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement, notes Inside Climate News.

Against this grim backdrop, New York’s Museum of Modern Art is announcing that it will give an annual grant totaling $200,000 in recognition of a single project by architects whose work is, as the award name has it, “nature-reconciled.” The prize comes with a $100,000 cash purse for the winner; it also includes another $100,000 that will go to a nonprofit organization to plant trees in the project client’s name. The prize is named the Ambasz-MoMA prize in return for a major gift from the Legacy Emilio Ambasz Foundation. It will recognize projects created anywhere in the world in the last three decades that “repair architecture’s relationship with nature,” as the museum puts it in press materials.

The museum bills it as the largest award for a single project in the field of architecture. The $100,000 cash component equals that of the Pritzker Architecture Prize, which honors living architects for significant achievement. The full $200,000 award equals the Driehaus Prize, given annually by the University of Notre Dame to a living architect working in traditional and classical architectural forms.

An Argentinian-American architect, Ambasz has had a longstanding relationship with the museum, having served as a curator in the architecture and design department between 1968 and 1976. He has contributed over $20 million total to the museum, and has served on its International Council since 1978; he served on the board of directors at MoMA PS1 from 2002 to 2006. He has won architecture awards, including one for the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan.

In the inaugural year, Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA, an architecture firm based in Dhaka, Bangladesh, takes home the prize for its Friendship Centre, in Gaibandha, Bangladesh. Designed between 2008 and 2010 and completed in 2011, it is a training facility and meeting space for “underserved communities” in the flood-prone rural Jamuna River delta, which is also susceptible to earthquakes.

As the soil there cannot bear large weights, which would otherwise necessitate costly elevated foundations, the Friendship Centre instead employs a compacted earthen embankment to protect it from floods. It was built by hand almost exclusively with clay bricks made locally by area workers. Its form and style were inspired partly by the ruins of a monastery at nearby Mahasthangarh, the earliest known archaeological site and oldest city in the country, dating back to at least the third century BCE.

“The Friendship Centre has been in service to an underserved community for 14 years. Yet, it is not a building of 14 years of age, but rather 2,300 years of age, as it draws its inspiration for flood protection from the nearby third-century BC settlement of Mahasthan,” said Chowdhury in press materials. “We are delighted that its coexistence with the surrounding agricultural, rural landscape, without really showing its mass forms to adjoining villages, has been recognized in this important judgment.” Chowdhury established his firm in partnership with Marina Tabassum in 1995 and has been principal since 2005. He was the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Friendship Centre in the 2014–16 cycle, as well as qualifying as a finalist for the same award in 2004 for A5, a pavilion apartment.

The Centre, which includes offices, classrooms, a library, meditation spaces, dormitories, and dining facilities. It also employs green roofs, open-air courtyards, and interconnected rainwater harvesting pools to moderate temperatures and provide natural ventilation. Mean temperatures can range into the mid-90s in April and May, with relative humidity averaging between 65 and 74 percent.

The other $100,000 will go to the Fundación Gran Chaco in Formosa, Argentina, which will contribute to reforestation efforts in the Gran Chaco forest in honor of Friendship, the NGO founded and directed by Runa Khan, who commissioned the Friendship Centre.

The Friendship Centre was chosen from a pool of nearly 140 projects, developed through research by the Ambasz Institute along with nominations by 30 international experts nominating candidates from their own regions.

The Emilio Ambasz Institute for the Joint Study of the Built and Natural Environment was established in 2020 and is housed in MoMA’s department of architecture and design. It organized the 2023–24 exhibition “Emerging Ecologies: Architecture and the Rise of Environmentalism.” e-flux wrote that “the exhibition imagines an alternative American future where nature is in harmony with human settlement—technologically, aesthetically, and spiritually,” and called it “a brilliant cross-section of architectural innovations as they were developed.”

“This inaugural prize marks an important extension of the Institute’s research beyond the Museum, recognizing exemplary architectural practice while supporting tangible environmental action,” said Evangelos Kotsioris, director of the Emilio Ambasz Institute and an architecture and design curator at MoMA, in press materials. “By honoring Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA’s extraordinary work on the Friendship Centre, the inaugural Ambasz–MoMA Prize recognizes an architecture that brings together environmental adaptation, historical continuity, and an extraordinary sensitivity to the communities it serves.”

Serving on the inaugural prize jury along with Kotsioris were Martino Stierli, chief curator of architecture and design, and Paula Vilaplana de Miguel, assistant curator of architecture and design. Two distinguished external jury members—Shelley McNamara, of Ireland’s Grafton Architects and Wang Shu, of China’s Amateur Architecture Studio—joined the museum’s jury.

item.title: Lorna Simpson Wins $105,000 Wolfgang Hahn Prize - ARTnews.com
item.description:
American artist Lorna Simpson, who pioneered a new approach to conceptual photography, has been named the winner of the 2027 Wolfgang Hahn Prize. The Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany, which sponsors the annual prize, will put €100,000 (about $105,000) toward the acquisition of a work by Simpson for its collection. A solo exhibition of her work will staged by the institution next year, accompanied by a publication.

The 2027 award jury comprised Naomi Beckwith, deputy director and chief curator of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and artistic director of documenta 16, and the Museum Ludwig board.

Born in Brooklyn, Simpson rose to international renown in the 1990s with multilayered photographs that pair images with fragmented text. Her practice eventually expanded to encompass film, painting, drawing, and sculpture, often blending the boundaries between mediums while remaining focused on inner worlds and popular perceptions of Black women.

Her two-part photo-text work ID (1990) was included in Museum Ludwig’s 1999 group exhibition “Art Worlds in Dialogue (Kunstwelten im Dialog).” In that work, Simpson paired two portraits of a Black woman. In one, she turns her back to the camera; a plaque bearing the word “identity” is mounted alongside the image. The other reveals only the crown of her head, which resembles the Earth emerging from deep space. A plaque engraved with the word “identify” is mounted over this image. The museum’s catalog text from 1999 compared ID to the Black Madonna of Cologne, a famous wooden statute and site of pilgrimage housed in a 17th-century church near the institution.

“Her multifaceted body of work will provide, in the jury’s view, an important impetus for the Museum Ludwig’s collection of American art,” the museum said in a statement.

The statement continued that the acquisition “will further develop the positions in Pop Art and its use of media-influenced imagery, which Peter and Irene Ludwig acquired early on and in considerable depth.” The museum described Simpson’s work as “a bridge” to the practices of Diamond Stingily and Carolyn Lazard, whose works newly entered its collection through the Junger Ankauf initiative and “reflect on the self-image of African American women.”

Established in 1994, the Wolfgang Hahn Prize honors established contemporary artists with internationally recognized bodies of work who are not yet widely known in Germany. Previous recipients include Lee Ufan, Francis Alÿs, Kerry James Marshall, Betye Saar, Frank Bowling, and Haegue Yang.

item.title: Human Rights Orgs Denounce Egypt's Arrest of Mada Masr Editor Lina Attalah - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, co-founder and editor-in-chief of Egypt's independent news outlet Mada Masr, is facing a one-year prison sentence among other penalties in a targeted crackdown on press freedom.

Summoned to court in Cairo last month on charges of publishing false news and operating the news site without a license, Attalah learned during the proceedings that she had been handed a year-long sentence in absentia on similar charges in 2024 without her knowledge.

Human rights and press freedom organizations, including Reporters Without Borders, Human Rights Watch, and the International Federation for Human Rights, have publicly condemned the charges against the journalist and Mada Masr, decrying her prosecution as a “Kafkaesque miscarriage of justice.”

item.title: Vienna Actionism Museum to Cease Exhibition Program Following Controversial Otto Muehl Show - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Vienna Actionism Museum will end its exhibition program in 2027 and transition into a research institution dedicated to the transgressive postwar art movement, Monopol reports. The research institution will be open to the public by appointment only.

The privately owned institution has been a controversial presence in Austria’s art scene since opening in 2024, owing to its focus on a movement known for violent, visceral performances that often used blood and excrement as materials. But public discontent escalated into outrage earlier this year, after the museum announced that its fall exhibition would be dedicated to the work of prominent Actionist Otto Muehl, who was convicted in 1991 of crimes including the sexual abuse of minors living in a commune he led throughout the 1970s and ’80s. The show opened on September 10 and will be on view through January 10, 2027.

Muehl reentered the art scene with apparent ease after his release in 1997, receiving exhibitions at prominent Viennese institutions, including the Museum of Applied Arts, the Leopold Museum, and the gallery W&K – Wienerroither & Kohlbacher. His market surged after his death in 2014, with his works continuing to fetch six-figure prices at galleries and auction houses throughout the 2010s, according to the Artnet Price Database.

This year made clear that Muehl’s legacy was no longer so easily defended. The Vienna Actionism Museum’s exhibition, titled “Otto Muehl: Art at the Abyss,” reignited debate in Austria over the presentation of his work, particularly after several living survivors of the commune spoke out against the show. Mathilda, a group led by former commune members, called on the institution financially divest from Muehl’s work, and on the Austrian government to investigate how the commune functioned with impunity for nearly two decades. In September, protesters organized under Mathilda gathered outside the museum, displaying large banners bearing the German phrases “Pedophile criminal and cult leader” and “Perpetrator’s museum.”

Despite the backlash, the museum appeared to stand by the exhibition. “Otto Muehl is one of the major figures of Austrian, European postwar art,” Klaus Albrecht Schroeder, the show’s curator and the director of the Vienna Actionism Museum, told the New York Times. “Talking about Muehl’s artistic importance doesn’t diminish the gravity of his crimes, and acknowledging his crimes doesn’t erase his place in art history.”

Muehl’s performances, spanning the 1960s through his arrest in 1990, are documented in photographs that capture the hallmarks of his practice: nudity, violence, and provocation. Like many of his Actionist peers, Muehl frequently staged group performances. Over time, however, his artistic practice became inextricably entangled with the criminal activity at the commune, raising difficult ethical questions about how his work should be studied and the complicity involved in its continued sale.

Ruth Bourgogne, a former commune member, has said that Muehl’s series of paintings known as “Rutschbilder,” or “Sliding Pictures,” were made by painting on the bodies of girls he had sexually abused and dragging them across the canvas. “The pictures look beautiful, but they are horrific; you can’t see the suffering on their faces, but it’s inside them,” she said during a public debate at the Vienna Festival last year. Another former commune member, who remained anonymous, recounted being sexually abused from the age of three. A nude photograph taken of her when she was 12 was later sold at a prominent Viennese auction house, a sale she described as agonizing to watch.

The “sliding” works are not included in the Vienna Actionism Museum’s exhibition, though they continue to attract interest at auction: one sold for €25,000 (roughly $29,000) in 2020. According to the museum, it only exhibited works created before the founding of the commune in 1970. The museum’s founder, art dealer Philipp Konzett acquired a trove of Muehl’s works from the Friedrichshof Cooperative, which was run by former commune members after the commune’s collapse. Museum director Julia Moebus-Puckener Activismus has defended its mission as not “glorifying perpetrators” and stated that the institution does not sell paintings.

The museum exhibited a wide range of work made by the central figures of Viennese Actionism, including Günter Brus, Hermann Nitsch, and Rudolf Schwarzkogler. Work by Muehl, however, accounted for a large part of the museum’s collection. Museum shareholders said in a statement today that the “justified moral condemnation” of Muehl now overshadows his artistic legacy, making an exhibition of his work no longer viable.

Muehl expressed regret for certain offenses in 2010, on the occasion of a major retrospective at the Leopold Museum. He struck a less contrite tone in a 2004 interview with Die Zeit, in which he characterized his convictions as “character assassination” and described the teenagers he sexually abused as “fully developed girls.”

ARTnews has contacted the museum for comment.

item.title: American Novelist and Four Others to Stand Trial Over Sale of Gold Looted from Shipwreck - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a story that sounds ripped from the pages of a novel, an American novelist, her husband, and three French nationals are set to stand trial in France next May for their alleged involvement in the resale of gold bars looted from an 18th-century shipwreck decades ago.

Eleanor “Gay” Courter, 82, an author of best-selling fiction, nonfiction, and memoir; her husband, Philip Courter, 84, a film director; Yves Gladu, 79, a professional underwater photographer; his wife, Brigitte Gladu, 76; and his sister-in-law, Annette May Pesty, 80, have all been charged with conspiracy. Some also face charges of money laundering and receiving stolen goods.

According to her website, Gay Courter has mainly written historical fiction and thrillers. And in case you were wondering, none of her books has a plot involving gold looted from a mysterious shipwreck.

The case will go before a criminal court in Brest on May 27, 2027, Agence France-Presse reported.

The case begins with the 1974 discovery of Le Prince de Conty, a French trading ship that sank off the coast of Brittany in 1746. The wreck was found 30 to 50 feet underwater near the island of Belle-Île-en-Mer. After gold bullion was discovered there, the site was looted in 1975. Lawsuits tied up the wreck until the mid-1980s, according to France’s Department of Underwater Archaeological Research (DRASSM). In 1985, archaeologists resumed excavations to the site and recovered Chinese porcelain dating to the 18th century, tea crates, and three ingots of Chinese gold. However that same year, a storm battered the ship and the wreck was reburied.

The current investigation began in 2018, when Michel L’Hour, then-director of DRASSM, reported a suspicious sale of five gold ingots on the website of a US auction house. L’Hour told US officials he believed the ingots came from Le Prince de Conty. The objects were seized and returned to France in 2022.

Investigators identified Gay Courter as the seller of the ingots. She said Pesty and Pesty’s late partner, Gérard, had given her the gold. Pesty, for her part, had appeared with the gold on Antiques Roadshow in 1999 and said she found it while diving near Cape Verde. Investigators found that story implausible and turned their attention to Yves Gladu.

In 2022, while in custody, Gladu confessed to looting 16 gold bars from Le Prince de Conty over 40 dives to the site between 1976 and 1999. He said he had sold the gold in 2006 to a retired military officer living in Switzerland, and he denied any connection to the Courters. Investigators found, however, that Gladu had known the Courters since the 1980s and had vacationed with them three times.

The Courters were detained in 2022 and placed under house arrest. Investigators found that the couple had at one point held at least 23 gold bars and had sold 18 of them for nearly $200,000. The Courters say the money was meant to go to Gladu. Last year, their lawyer, Grégory Lévy, told the Guardian that the couple had no idea the gold was looted and “didn’t see the harm as in the United States regulations for gold are completely different from those in France.” He said they did not profit from the sales.

Earlier this week, Lévy told AFP that he will argue for the Courters’ acquittal. The Gladus declined to comment to AFP on the trial.

item.title: Christie’s Posts Highest Watch Total Ever and Sells Bulgari Pink Diamond for $14 M. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The luxury market continues to be a major area of growth for the auction houses. Christie’s is holding its luxury sales week in Geneva, its biggest such event for jewelry and watches, and while the house hasn’t released its final totals for the week, early returns appear promising.

On Monday, Christie’s reported that its Rare Watches sale, held at the Four Seasons Hotel des Bergues, generated $58.7 million on 218 lots with a 100 percent sell-through rate by lot. That’s more than double the equivalent sale in November 2025, which generated $27 million on 179 lots with a 99% sell-through rate.

Leading the sale was a trio of F.P. Journe Vagabondage I, II, and III watches in pink gold, which together brought in CHF 6.7 million ($8.2 million). Each one sold for well over its high estimate of CHF 800,000 ($976,000): the Vagabondage I went for CHF 2 million ($2.4 million), the Vagabondage II for CHF 2.2 million ($2.6 million), and the Vagabondage III for CHF 2.5 million ($3.1 million). The Vagabondage is a blue-chip watch by independent watchmaker F.P Journe, highly desired for its wandering digital display and produced in extremely limited numbers.

Christie’s Magnificent Jewels sale, meanwhile, generated $49.7 million on 112 lots. The top lot, a 24-carat Fancy Intense Pink emerald-cut diamond ring by Bulgari, sold for $14.8 million, squarely within its $12 million–$18 million estimate. That total fell well short of the $75 million achieved on 108 lots at the equivalent 2025 sale. That sale’s total, however, got a considerable boost from the Mellon Blue diamond, which accounted for $25.6 million of the take. Excluding the top lot from both sales reveals a slightly smaller but still significant decline: the remaining 111 lots this year brought in $34.9 million, down about 29 percent from the $49.4 million generated by the other 107 lots in 2025.

Still, one suspects that the auction house isn’t too worried. In July, Christie’s released its first-half totals for 2026, reporting that it posted its strongest six months 2021 with a overall total of $4.5 billion. Luxury sales, which includes watches and jewelry, were up 15 percent to $539 million.

Whether the second half of 2026 ends up as strong as Christie’s first half will ultimately depend on its marquee evening sales next week in New York, where some 850 artworks will hit the block and are expected to generate over $800 million. Luxury is on the rise, but for now, fine art is still king.

item.title: Peter Morris Architects’ Pastel Pink ‘Cloud House’ Billows in Northwest London - Colossal
item.description:
A confection of arches and windows has emerged in the Gospel Oak neighborhood of Camden in northwest London, thanks to Peter Morris Architects and a unique collaborative ownership approach. “The Cloud House,” which actually comprises two side-by-side townhomes, practically froths from its foundations. One side is occupied by the architect himself along with his partner, Emily, while the other half is owned by a resident who embraced the stylistic potential of the project and agreed to the exterior design and the same contractor.

Ten years in the making, “The Cloud House” is a playful response to its eclectic neighboring architecture, from the quirky Victorian church of St. Martin’s to a school next door that has a stone exterior mimicking a castle. Morris conceived of a bright, whimsical design with pink walls, robin’s egg-blue window frames and doors, and arched details in relief made from a dense recyclable polystyrene that mirrors the arches of the church across the street. See more on the firm’s Instagram.

item.title: Newark Museum Is Latest Art Institution to Transfer Ownership of David Drake Vessel - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The latest institution to transfer its ownership of a David Drake vessel in its collection is New Jersey’s Newark Museum of Art, which said on Thursday that the artist’s descendants were given possession of an 1852 jug.

Other museums have undertaken a similar measure, from the Museum of Fine Arts Boston to the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts. But the Newark Museum said in its release that, unlike past ownership transfers, this one was initiated by the institution, which reached out to Drake’s descendants, rather than the other way around.

Drake is now widely recognized for the stoneware jugs he produced during the 19th century in Edgefield, South Carolina. He was born into enslavement and achieved freedom sometime after the Civil War. The jugs, which memorably figured in a 2022 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition, sometimes bore written messages whose meaning has often been debated. One vessel by him topped ARTnews’s list of the best artworks about America earlier this year.

The Newark Museum work was inscribed with the date “March 14, 1852,” and was signed by Drake—under a version of his first name, Dave—along with the initials LM. Those initials reference Lewis Miles, on whose plantation Drake was enslaved. It is displayed galleries for 18th- and 19th-century American art, and will remain on view while the ownership is transferred.

Over the summer, the museum reached out to Drake’s descendants. A release said that now, “with full support of the board of trustees,” the jug’s ownership was given over to the family and subsequently repurchased.

Lisa Funderbunke, the Newark Museum’s director and CEO, said in a statement, “We are deeply grateful to David Drake’s descendants for their trust and partnership. Restoring ownership of this work is an important act of justice, one that is rooted in accountability, repair and healing, and reflects the values guiding NMOA’s next chapter. As the Museum enters a new era, we are honored to continue sharing Drake’s legacy with the public in partnership with his family.”

Yaba Barker, Drake’s fourth great-grandson, said in a statement, “For over 175 years, our ancestor’s vessels have carried stories and history that must be told. Thanks to this agreement, our family’s mission for Dave’s work to be accessible to the public, and for viewers to recognize us as Dave’s heirs and owners of his legacy, is being fulfilled by Newark Museum’s leadership, and we are so grateful.”

Though the Newark Museum did not report a price for repurchasing the jug, Eileen Kinsella reported in the Art Newspaper that the transaction will cost “around $135,000,” a figure that is considerably lower than Drake’s auction record.

item.title: $160,000 Hans Arp Sculpture Stolen From Art Cologne - Hyperallergic
item.description:
German police are seeking answers about the theft of Hans (Jean) Arp's “S’élevant (Rising)” (1962) from Gallery Ludorff's booth at Art Cologne, which went missing from its plinth on the last day of the blue-chip fair on Sunday, November 8, between 4:55pm and 5:10pm.

Since the fair kicked off on November 5, Arp's work had been sitting atop a plinth at the Düsseldorf gallery's booth, sandwiched between two paintings by Ernst Wilhelm Nay. Four employees were at the stand on November 8 and immediately notified the North Rhine-Westphalia State Police upon noticing that the unbolted sculpture, which is valued at €145,000 (~$160,000), had gone missing. As it remains unclear who made off with the 28-centimeter-tall (~11 in) sculpture, police are seeking any information or photographs from visitors or staffers that could aid in the investigation.

item.title: Hiroshi Sato’s Art Against Enshittification - Hyperallergic
item.description:
SAN FRANCISCO — What does reality look like in the age of AI? For the San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato, representational figurative painting is the antidote to our rapid loss of touch with what’s real and what isn’t. His stylistic blend of Bay Area Figurative Movement stylings and Edward Hopper-esque compositions creates an uneasy and uncanny portrait of what it feels like to be alive today — and might offer a way out of the simulacrum we all seem trapped in.

But Sato wasn’t always motivated by a desire to return to the real. He credits the COVID-19 pandemic with shifting his outlook on both politics and painting.

“Before COVID, my practice wasn’t about subject matter at all,” he told me when I visited him in his cramped Mission District studio in San Francisco, one of the last such buildings in the neighborhood artists were pushed out of during the dot-com boom. “When the pandemic happened, I realized that you can’t just keep making work that appears to be immune from time and what’s happening around you.”

item.title: Rembrandt’s “Night Watch” Is Alive! - Hyperallergic
item.description:
AMSTERDAM — It must have been a peculiar sight at the Rijksmuseum’s Gallery of Honor, where Rembrandt’s “The Night Watch” (1642) is the proud centerpiece: a microbiologist in a white lab coat, carefully taking samples of the canvas and placing them in prepared Petri dishes. “To get that close to the painting was very scary,” Eline van Bloois, the microbiologist in question, told Hyperallergic. “After all, it’s a piece of art that is so well-known to so many people.”

The Amsterdam institution has teamed up with an unlikely partner: ARTIS, the city’s zoo. Or, more specifically, with ARTIS-Micropia, the zoo’s science museum, focused on the study of microbes. Their scientists are researching what invisible life exists on what is arguably the most famous work in the Rijksmuseum’s collection. The findings are on display at The Night Watch Lives, which opened at ARTIS-Micropia on November 11.

A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt’s Dutch Golden Age masterpiece now adorns the wall at ARTIS-Micropia; different patches of the painting indicate with a number and a date that a sample was taken from there, and when. On a glass display in front of it, the Petri dishes are spread out, showing the microbes in all their splendor and revealing exactly which microorganisms have been found on the canvas.

The first results revealed, among other findings, bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots, and well-known skin bacteria meant to protect us against pathogens. But one that stood out immediately was the Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan. How this Japanese microorganism ended up on the Dutch “Night Watch,” or when, is a guessing game. 

“This is how it often goes with science,” Van Bloois said, “you start off with one question. You leave with a hundred.” 

The installation is still growing in scope. Six microbial trips to the Rijksmuseum have been scheduled, and merely three have been taken thus far. There are 20 bacterial findings currently on display. “There are 10 of them in the incubator right now; they’re brooding and still need to be identified,” said Karlien Pijnenborg, head of the adjoining Groote Museum, who leads the project. “And once they return, they’ll get a name tag and join the others. At the end, there’ll be 60.” 

The installation, which will be on display until the end of May, won’t be fully formed until sometime in February. “We want to have taken multiple samples,” said Van Bloois, “so we really have gone over the entire painting.” 

ARTIS-Micropia is the first museum dedicated solely to microbes. “It’s such a niche museum, it mostly attracts people who love and know a lot about microbiology,” said Pijnenborg. “But you of course want everyone to get interested in it, because microbes are so important.”

Most of all, the museum wants microbes to get less of a bad rap out there. “We know a lot about microbes that can make you sick,” said Van Bloois, “but that is only about 1% of all microbes we know.” 

According to the museum, it’s the first time this kind of microbial research has been conducted on a piece of art. When Rembrandt finished “The Night Watch” in 1642, microbes hadn’t even been discovered yet. “It really was a whimsical idea of ours,” Pijnenborg said.

The research coincides with Operation Night Watch, the largest and most wide-ranging restoration and research project ever undertaken on the masterpiece, launched in 2019. In 2023, scientists working in the initiative discovered a rare lead compound in the layer underneath the primer. The researchers suspect Rembrandt applied this to better protect the canvas against mold and other microbes, as “The Night Watch” would be hung on a damp exterior wall.

Right now, the restorers are removing old layers of varnish, a process that can be witnessed live at the Rijksmuseum from behind a glass partition. The operation will continue for years to come. 

The research conducted by ARTIS-Micropia fits perfectly within Operation Night Watch. As for the Rijksmuseum, they consider the microbial research strengthening for the arts, too. 

“Thirty or forty years ago, nobody could have imagined you’d be talking to a chemist or biologist about ‘The Night Watch,’” said Taco Dibbits, the Rijksmuseum’s director, during a press conference. “And I think precisely because this research is broadening — the fact that the humanities and the exact sciences are collaborating — it also leads to it becoming more widely embraced.

item.title: Get Up-Close to Cells, Ink, and Insects in the Nikon Small World Photomicrography Contest - Colossal
item.description:
From fungi and insects to technology and crystals, the winning entries in the 2026 Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition reveal astonishing details typically invisible to the naked eye. This year’s top prize went to Ole Bielfeldt, a student and experimental photographer based in Cologne, Germany, who used a hand-built rig to capture an incredible up-close view of droplets inside of an inkjet printer. Runners-up included John-Oliver Dum’s portrait of a jumping spider with pollen on its body and Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery’s capture of mouse neurons.

Winner images were organized into three categories: Top 20, Honorable Mentions, and Images of Distinction. Explore some of our favorites here, and head to the contest’s website to see all of this year’s best photos. You might also enjoy the Nikon Small World in Motion video competition.

item.title: With Protests Quieting Down But Not Forgotten, Dealers Return to the Grand Palais for Paris Photo - ARTnews.com
item.description:
As soft music crooned through the halls of a softly lit, glittering Grand Palais in Paris Tuesday evening, VIPs trickled in for a private dinner hosted by the Prix Pictet as part of the Paris Photo fair, which opens to the public on November 12. Wandering through the fair’s aisles featuring 246 exhibitors this year, it was unsettling to imagine that just three weeks ago, Art Basel Paris had to evacuate the very same venue. Booths were dismantled early, the night before protests planned for October 24. The fair’s closure two days sooner than planned was unprecedented and came as a shock to many, ultimately necessitating Art Basel to offer a 20 percent discount on booth fees to all exhibitors.

Though civil unrest in France has not returned to the fever pitch experienced in October, and the government has exerted some greater control over the situation, demonstrations are continuing here, in an effort to bring attention to rising costs of living and under-funded public schools. How then, are Paris Photo organizers and exhibitors navigating it all?

“We are, of course, watching the situation closely to see how things evolve,” Photo Paris director Florence Bourgeois told ARTnews. “At this stage there is nothing new to report, and nothing alarming. In fact, for two weeks the demonstrations have been taking place peacefully, and generally in the east of Paris. So we are not alarmed, and we remain vigilant so that we can respond if necessary.”

Bourgeois said that the fair has closed early once before, after the 2015 terror attacks in Paris; despite lacking appropriate insurance at the time, organizers reimbursed 20 percent of booth fees. “But that’s no indication of what might happen in 2026,” she said. “It was an extremely different situation to that of the current protests.” (She declined to comment further on the fair’s current insurance policy.)

“If we ever do face something along those lines, our decision would be made based on protecting everyone’s safety. That’s the priority,” she added.

For German gallerist Thomas Zander, who exhibited at the shortened Art Basel Paris and is now back for Paris Photo, the city is the biggest draw. “It’s strange in a way, but I love Paris,” he said about returning so soon. He characterized this year’s Art Basel Paris as inspiring a “difficult feeling” in him. The early closure cost him “two good days” of sales, he said, adding, “Now we are in a better situation this week, and there are not so many demonstrations in the center, and it’s quieter than the week of Art Basel Paris.”

At the fair, his booth has on view what he described as “museum-quality works” because “all the museum people come here, to Paris Photo.” This includes a set of six dye transfer unique master prints by William Eggleston from 1968 to 1973, priced together at €1 million ($1.11 million); a rare series of 41 vintage gelatin silver prints of pinball machines by Candida Höfer, which are being sold as a single display for €600,000 ($665,570); and 16 works from Zoe Leonard’s “Analogue” series (1998–2009) about New York’s changing Lower East Side and offered for a total of €140,000 ($155,300).

In terms of price point, Paris Photo is a much more accessible fair than Art Basel Paris, where artworks are frequently offered in the six-, seven-, and even eight-figures. While some exhibitors at Paris Photo might make a sale over $1 million, the prices for other works can start as low as a few hundred dollars, with artist-signed books even costing under $100.

Despite having lower prices than the markets for contemporary painting and sculpture, the photography market has not been immune to the rest of the cooling that the global art market has faced in the past few years, according to Bourgeois, who said that more than ever closing a sale “comes down to a question of quality, which is why we’ve worked hard to represent the best that photography has produced over the last 200 years.” Even still, “for top quality photographic works, prices remain high and are not falling,” she added.

Several dealers said that approachability and a perceived distancing from the billionaire’s club of collectors often play to the favor of Paris Photo, as protestors demand greater social equality. (In October, there were calls to protest outside Art Basel Paris and “take back the Grand Palais” from the wealthy few.)

“By taking part in a fair, we are not ignoring the realities of life around us, nor disconnected from it,” Bourgeois said. “We also represent part of the economy: there are galleries that make a living from this, that represent artists, give them visibility and support them by selling their work. I believe all of this is very important.”

“I’ve been hearing from a lot of people that Paris Photo doesn’t have quite the same image as Art Basel,” Paris dealer Anne-Laure Buffard said. “It’s a fair that has less of a connotation symbolizing a certain concentration of wealth, or an elitism reserved for the extremely rich.” With the recent closure in mind, in light of the protesters who have calmed, Buffard said, “We’re all trying to stay optimistic.”

She is presenting salt-washed and painted, crystalline photographs taken in the Dead Sea, on the border between Israel, Jordan, and the West Bank, by Ilanit Illouz, priced from about $2,000 to $17,750; as well as painted and drawn photographs by Vasantha Yogananthan chronicling the impact of tourism on the northern Indian region of the Himalayas, priced between about $3,300 and $11,100.

Elsewhere, Pace Gallery is offering a jewel of a 1926 vintage gelatin silver print on a treated postcard by André Kertész for $500,000. It is thought to be one of only six or seven in the world. On the more affordable end, medium-sized still life photographs by Kiki Smith have already sold for $8,500 apiece.

“It’s been a very strong first day, with a number of significant sales made in the first hours of the fair, reflecting the strong demand for photography,” Pace senior vice president Lauren Panzo said. “It’s particularly encouraging to see so many new collectors coming through” alongside existing clients.

On Tuesday evening, Panzo told ARTnews that while the gallery has considered the possibility of further interruptions to the fair from ongoing protests, she is “personally not concerned—there are always protests here,” and the current ones seem to be more “under control.” She expects that over the weekend there will be lines to get into the Grand Palais as there have been in years past. “People in Paris love photography. I think there’s such a love for this medium. It’s so accessible,” she said. “Photography is different.”

Greeting visitors upon entering the Grand Palais is a large installation of works spanning the career of German photographer Thomas Ruff, a collaboration by his five galleries: David Zwirner, Konrad Fischer, Mai 36, Lia Rumma, Sprüth Magers. Other highlights include a selection spotlighting women photographers, who now make up 38 percent of artists represented at the fair, up from 20 percent when the program launched in 2018, and around 100 newly acquired and unseen photographs from the Centre Pompidou’s collection. The Prix Pictet also now has a dedicated booth, featuring works by this year’s winner: Valérie Belin’s Still Life, showing an accumulation of plastic goods and memento mori, and Alfredo Jaar’s The End, which documents the receding Great Salt Lake in Utah.

A curated selection of artworks spread throughout the Grand Palais represents every decade since the creation of photography, which is marking its 200th anniversary this year. On one end are Serge Plantureux and Atelier 41, which have on view works by the pioneer photographer, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, who made what is considered the world’s oldest known existing photograph, View from the Window at Le Gras (1825).

Among contemporary examples in the Voices section is an installation of new works by Alessandro Calabrese in the booth of Milan’s Viasaterna gallery. Priced between $2,440 and $8,430, these dreamy images are made by printing on the “wrong” side of glossy photo paper, resulting in painterly, electric-hued prints. “In the end, it creates a sort of watercolor painting, but [made] automatically,” Calabrese told ARTnews. “All my research is based on looking for the limit of the figurative side and the realism in photography, and trying to challenge it.”

item.title: After a Historic Electoral Rout, Trump Again Asks the Supreme Court to Greenlight His Ballroom - ARTnews.com
item.description:
One day after the historic rout by the Democrats nationwide on Election Day a week ago, Trump took to the construction site of the sprawling ballroom he is constructing on the grave of the East Wing of the White House, which he abruptly razed in October 2025. “Trump invited reporters into a cavernous construction site and talked about the building project for nearly 20 minutes,” reported PBS, “without mentioning sweeping Republican defeats around the country the night before.”

The next day, Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed a petition asking the Supreme Court to greenlight the 90,000-square-foot construction project, including the 22,000-square-foot ballroom-cum-military complex. He asked the justices to rule on whether a district court, at the behest of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, erred in August in enjoining the ongoing “renovation” of the East Wing. The $400 million project has been the subject of heated debate and lawsuits since its inception. Sauer asks that the court reverse a lower court’s ruling outright or hear oral arguments, explains SCOTUSblog.

The petition starts off by claiming the injunction was granted “at the behest of a single passerby claiming she will dislike how the new building looks.” That passerby was Alison K. Hoagland, a member of the board of the National Trust for Historic Preservation. The question of whether she has legal standing to sue is a central issue in the ongoing argument.

Sauer claims she has no standing, because the court has ruled that “mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury.” He further calls the ballroom a “vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” arguing that it is necessary because the president faces “an onslaught of assassination attempts.” (There have been, counting generously, three.)

A consultation with the Secret Service and the National Parks Service, says the petition, determined that demolition and rebuilding would be the most cost-effective course of action and would be best “to ensure that the East Wing remains minimally visible from public spaces.”

The old structure couldn’t support the ballroom’s necessary security features, says the White House, including blast-proof windows, fortified walls, and missile-resistant columns. Nor could the underground military installation be built under the existing structure.

In April 2026, US District Court judge Richard J. Leon wrote a searing 35-page opinion, employing some 18 exclamation marks, rejecting Trump’s plan for the ballroom, saying that “the President of the United States is the steward of the White House for future generations of First Familes. He is not, however, the owner!”

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia froze Leon’s order to allow the court time to consider the government’s appeal, outlines SCOTUSblog. A three-judge panel upheld Leon’s ruling in August but pushed its effective date back two weeks to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court. The majority wrote that only Congress has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures.” A dissenting judge said Hoagland had no standing.

The Trump administration called Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” and Sauer asked the justices to pause the ruling, saying construction was “vitally required by national security” and that Hoagland’s “dislike” for the new construction doesn’t constitute a legal injury.

In August, a federal court ruled that Trump lacked the authority to build without Congressional approval, but the Supreme Court greenlighted the construction project in a stay issued by Chief Justice John Roberts; the Court ruled 5–4 for the White House on August 31. Roberts dissented and, along with Ketanji Brown Jackson, Elena Kagan, and Sonia Sotomayor, ruled that the construction “is likely unlawful” and that the majority decision was “no victory for the separation of powers” and that Hoagland did have standing.

In any event, there’s no turning back now, says Sauer, writing that the project is 70% complete, “and, in turn (sic), there remains no sound way now to redesign or unwind the massive superstructure that is currently standing at the White House.”

item.title: Art Bros About to Get More Insufferable as Artnet Partners With Kalshi - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In a new low for an art world we thought had reached rock bottom, Artnet has announced an official partnership with the betting platform Kalshi in an incestuous marriage of two markets known for financial opacity, insider trading, and the most insufferable straight men you've ever met: art and predictions.

The news came in a press release ahead of New York's marquee auction week, promising interested budding criminals users an exclusive opportunity to “trade yes-or-no contracts in a peer-to-peer structure” (??) on public art sales. The mechanism is as follows: Artnet will use its Price Database, once nostalgically the realm of wannabe art advisors trying to sound like they have an MBA, to “curate" (help) “events” (HELP) such as whether a lot will exceed its estimate. Surprising no one, Miami Art Week in December will be the “next major moment” for the partnership, bro.

item.title: Piecing Together Romare Bearden’s Life - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A new documentary about Romare Bearden embraces a collage-like sensibility, fitting well with the artist’s most influential work. Romare Bearden: A Life in Collage, soon to screen at DOC NYC, eschews the familiar structure of a linear biography, jumping around to find thematic rhymes through different periods of Bearden’s life. 

Early on, for instance, the film alludes to Bearden’s family’s participation in the Great Migration, but rather than dwell on his biography, it turns to the recurring motif of trains in his work.

The film benefits from generous access to recordings of Bearden himself, who speaks with remarkable elegance about his memories, artistic process, and influences. Shaped by living in the South, Harlem, and Pittsburgh, his studies at the Sorbonne, and his time in the military and semiprofessional baseball during the first half of the 20th century, Bearden synthesized them into an oeuvre now seen as emblematic of the broader Black experience of the era.

item.title: Liverpool Biennial Announces Artist List and ‘Age of Magical Thinking’ Theme - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The 2027 edition of the Liverpool Biennial, scheduled to open June 5 and continue through September 19, will feature 25 artists and collectives assembled in mind of a newly designated theme: “The Age of Magical Thinking.”

“The title draws on psychologist Jean Piaget’s identification of a particular period in childhood development when the lines between reality and make-believe are blurred,” reads a press release. “This is an age when the imagination is powerful; tomorrow is charged with potential and when magical thinking can help to create new, alternative worlds.”

Curated by Aimee Harrison and Lucía Sanromán, the exhibition across the city in North West England will include a public art project created by local young people and artist Harold Offeh for Williamson Square as well as new commissioned works by Francis Alÿs, Tania Candiani, and Laakkuluk Williamson. Venues for the show include the Bluecoat, FACT Liverpool, Walker Art Gallery, Open Eye Gallery, Victoria Gallery & Museum, Liverpool Cathedral, and the Exhibition Research Laboratory at Liverpool John Moores University.

About the theme, Sanromán, the cocurator, said, “As someone deeply committed to socially engaged and participatory forms of art, working on a Biennial informed by the perspectives and experiences of children and young people has given Aimee and I a lens to view and face the complexity of this particularly uncertain political moment, globally.”

Harrison added, “We have an opportunity to learn alongside children about living in a world that is both hard and full of possibility.”

Below, see the complete list of artists and collectives to be included in the next Liverpool Biennial.
