item.title: Christie’s Brings a Blockbuster Klimt Landscape to Auction, Tagged at $80 M. and Guaranteed to Sell - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A major work by a market titan will go under the hammer at Christie’s New York next moth. Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915–1916) is estimated at $60–80 million, which, if achieved, would put it among the Austrian artist’s top prices at public sale. The piece is guaranteed to sell, the house confirmed to ARTnews. It has been in the same private collection for nearly three decades; the seller is unnamed. It goes to auction at the house’s marquee November 17 evening sale of 20th- and 21st-century art.

The painting set a record for Klimt when the family of the current owner paid $14.7 million for it at Sotheby’s New York in May 1997 (at that time, it was listed under the title Litzlbergkeller am Attersee, by which it has also been known); adjusted for inflation, that’s about $30.9 million. At that sale, it came from the estate of Serge Sabarasky, a cofounder of New York’s Neue Galerie, just a few subway stops north of Christie’s Rockefeller Center saleroom, where the work will be offered after a quick jaunt (October 27–29) to the auctioneer’s Hong Kong showroom. (As it happens, the Neue Galerie, home to some major Klimt works, reopens November 12 after a construction project.)

“The inn of Litzlbergkeller sits at the water’s edge, between Klimt’s allover technique and abstraction, form and dissolution, prewar certainties and the unknown,” said Max Carter, global chairman of 20th and 21st-century art, in press materials.

Klimt’s auction record stands at $236.4 million, paid at Sotheby’s New York in November 2025 for his Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16). Six of the Austrian’s top 10 prices at auction were fetched by landscapes; seven of his top 10 prices were notched in 2022 or after, helping to fuel a patchy art-market recovery weighted toward the top end, leading ARTnews to title its new Top 200 Collectors issue “The Year of the Trophy.”

From 1900 until his death in 1918, Klimt often spent his summers in the Austrian countryside on the shores of Lake Attersee, pictured in the canvas on offer. “It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world,” wrote Sarah Belmont for ARTnews in reviewing his top prices, some of which were for landscapes painted there.

The canvas on offer presents a view focused on the Litzlberg Cellar, a brewery and inn on the north shore where Klimt stayed during his first several summers in the area, but actually dates from a decade after his move to a cottage on the lake’s southern shore. The artist partly based the composition on his own study via a telescope from the opposite shore and partly on postcard views, Christie’s points out.

“This landscape reads like a lyrical composition in three stanze—the forest with majestic, whispering oak trees; the house embraced by their foliage; the shimmering reflection in the lake,” said Giovanna Bertazzoni, chairman of Christie’s Europe, in a press release, calling the work “inestimable.”

The piece was commissioned by banker and entrepreneur Otto Primavesi, who, with his wife Eugenia, was a major patron of the arts and commissioned Klimt to paint two family portraits in 1912. It went by 1927 to Austrian photographer and anthropologist Hugo Bernatzik; then to Vienna collector Kurt Wieser, who owned it from the ‘30s until at least 1958; and from there to Sabarsky, a major promoter of Klimt’s work.

In its long life, it has hung on the walls of museums and institutions such as Secession Vienna; the Künstlerhaus in Vienna; the Musées Royaux des Beaux-Arts in Brussels; Palazzo Strozzi in Venice; Kunsthaus Zürich; and the Leopold Museum in Vienna.

Christie’s announcement of the Klimt consignment comes just days after the same house announced another work with an $80 million high estimate: a Wassily Kandinsky abstraction that is guaranteed to exceed the Russian-born artist’s current high. Also in October, the house announced a $100 million group of works from a “distinguished collector” that is reported to be the famed artist Jeff Koons.

The auctioneer’s main competitor, Sotheby’s, has not been without major consignments for next month. It will offer $450 million in works from the Blaquier family, led by a major Vincent van Gogh; a $100 million collection of works from the estate of Ted and Ruth Baum, led by paintings by Mark Rothko and Ed Ruscha; and a dozen works from bankrupt Miami hedge funder George Allen Weiss.

item.title: 50 Artworks by Artists Who Lived and Worked in India Gifted to the Tate - ARTnews.com
item.description:
50 artworks from the collection of Charles Greig, a British academic and expert in Indian art, have been donated to the Tate. The collection includes oil paintings, watercolors and miniatures by artists who lived and worked in India during the 18th and 19th centuries.

The museum described the gift as an “entirely philanthropic act,” with Greig donating the works outright and without the use of tax incentives. Greig built the collection over four decades and features artists such as Sita Ram and Ghulam Ali Khan—who capitalized on the new market for their work among British East India Company officials—as well as European artists such as Johan Zoffany and Rudolf Swoboda, and British landscapists like William Hodges, Thomas Daniell and William Daniell. The works in the collection reflect India and Britain’s shared history and complex power dynamics between the two nations.

Greig said in a statement that the main focus of his collection was an exploration of the “deep and intricate relationship between Britain and the Indian subcontinent through the entwined complexities of the artistic encounter. Most of the works were made in the vanished world before photography and they provide us with a visual record of our rich shared history from about 1770.” He called assembling this collection his life’s “primary passion, but at no stage did I ever see myself as other than a temporary steward.”

Notable artworks in the collection include German painter Johan Zoffany’s Portrait of Prince Jawan Bakht (also known as Jahandar Shah) (1784), making it one of only three portraits of individual Indian sitters by the artist to be held in UK public collections; Austrian painter Rudolph Swoboda’s Sepoy in HH Maharaja Srinagar’s Indian Regiment, 23 Years Old (1886), painted for Queen Victoria, is the first work by the artist to enter a British museum collection. The three watercolors by Sita Ram draw on both Indian art traditions and European visual languages.

“These works encompass a unique cross-cultural discourse, it seems to me vital that they are preserved intact to be enjoyed and studied by all mankind. A collection built on a life of study deserves to be universally accessible and I am profoundly happy to see these works find a permanent home at Tate,” said Greig.

The collection is expected to be exhibited at the Tate Britain in 2028. Alex Farquharson, director of Tate Britain, said in a statement that the museum is “always looking to tell new and different stories about Britain’s role in international art history” and that this gift from Greig will “significantly strengthen our holdings of art produced in the British Empire and broaden the range of people and histories represented in the national collection.”

item.title: Walid Raad’s Way of Working Is Inspired by the Mirrors in Vampire Movies - ARTnews.com
item.description:
As a teenager, Walid Raad would walk around his hometown with a camera, just trying to make some sense of the world. At a glance, the black-and-white pictures he captured then offer cool, detached views. But he quickly discovered there was only so much sense to be made of war-torn Beirut. One day, walking by a bakery, he snapped a cake displayed in the window. It was decorated with birthday wishes for someone named Hassan. Only later, developing the film at home—his dad had converted the bathroom to a darkroom, encouraging his hobby—did Raad register the date: The cake was for Hassan Nasrallah, then a rising militiaman in the Lebanese Civil War. Raad briefly fantasized about poisoning it. “But I was 15,” he told me, laughing. “I was a coward.”

Decades later, with a PhD and a MoMA retrospective under his belt, Raad returned to that image in a series of digitally fabricated birthday cakes addressed to political leaders who feel difficult to celebrate: happy birthday to Ali, Kamal, Tony, Walid; joyeux anniversaire to Yasser, Elias, Nabih, Amine. By then, Nasrallah had become the leader of Hezbollah; in 2024, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike. Raad’s colorful cakes are at once cheerful and cold—his trademark tragicomic blend of fiction and fact. In his cakes, as in so much of his work, grand political events unfold on an intimate, human scale.

Begun, in a sense, when Raad was just 15, the cake project has everything of his signature: He starts with something true—a document—then extrapolates its logic to create something fictional, maybe even a little fantastical. That method has carried him through a nearly 40-year career and counting.

His work is a standout in the main show in this year’s Venice Biennale: His paintings, drawings, and photographs of banal-seeming beds spring to life when you read a wall text claiming that they were slept in by Yasser Arafat, who “is said to have never slept in the same bed two nights in a row.” The PLO leader survived more than 40 assassination attempts, and “he could not afford to throw caution to the wind… so he lived—and slept—on the move.” Raad adds that he has spent 30 years searching for the beds Arafat slept in, drafting paintings of his mattresses and duvets that he just couldn’t seem to complete.

With the beds and cakes alike, the story unfolds quite literally along the images’ edges: The paintings of the beds are incomplete, bordered with tape and brushstrokes. The birthday cakes appear pulled out of manila envelopes along with piles of pictures, as if being entered into evidence at a trial. Raad says he is “creating the documents I wished already existed.”

SINGLING OUT RAAD’S Arafat pictures in the Biennale, the scholar Saidiya Hartman described his “belief in the imaginative and the speculative” as “critical.” Hartman has devoted her life’s work to imagining the lives of oppressed people who left limited traces in the archive—people who were silenced or illiterate, people whose voices were only recorded under conditions of coercion, or people who necessarily lived clandestine lives—like Arafat. She calls her approach “critical fabulation.”

Indeed, Raad is best known for his own method of fabulation, marrying stories and pictures, imaginations and histories. This way of working has everything to do with his primary subject: the Arab world and its politics and conflicts—particularly the Lebanese Civil War (1975—90) that unfolded in Raad’s youth. While floods of images and their competing narratives have all but defined the digital age, this battleground of misinformation has had notable consequences in the region. “During the war,” remembers Khalil Joreige, another Lebanese artist exhibiting in the Venice Biennale this year, “every militia had its own media station, television, newspaper, or radio. There was a real war of images”—a war Joreige says influenced his generation’s “sophisticated relationship to images.”

Accordingly, the Harvard art historian Carrie Lambert-Beatty has described Raad’s work as an exemplar of “parafiction,” adding that one of the most powerful things art can do is get viewers to experience a given scenario as having been true—and remind them that other worlds are possible. In her recent book on artistic research, art historian Claire Bishop singled out Raad too, noting that, while so much work in the genre reproduces the experience of information overload—think: documents in vitrines—Raad offers synthesis in the form of narrative, all without collapsing into the trope of authoritative master narratives against which so much research-based art reacts.

In my own book, Fables & Forensics, I describe Raad’s work as a kind of surrealism for the information age, noting how he gives playful form to the ordinary if dizzying glut of misinformation—but adding that he does so without ever falling into the trap of reproducing fake news. Any fact—a bed, or a birthday cake—that could be mistaken for true is of little consequence, and there are always clues as to the constructed nature of his documents; just remember to look at the edges.

Raad is best known for the work he made as a fictional collective called the Atlas Group, work that presses on photography’s fraught relationship with truth. The Group’s video Hostage: The Bachar tapes (#17 and #31), which they attribute to the year 2000, sees Souheil Bachar narrate his experience of being held hostage in Lebanon from 1983 to ’93 alongside five Western men; he was the only Arab. Some scenes simply show Bachar against a white wall, though the video reveals itself as obviously manipulated by way of green-screened footage of Ronald Reagan. There are less obvious clues, too: If you don’t speak Arabic, you might miss how Bachar’s words are at times contradicted by the English translation.

The Group, Raad says, ran from 1989 to 2004. But dates, like all facts, are his medium. You’ll also find magazines and museums that trace the Group’s origin to 1967, the year of Raad’s birth, or to 1948, or 1945. And the Group has attributed archival images to nonexistent institutions—like the Museum of Fine Art New York. Both the Tate and the Museum of Modern Art in New York have acquired editions of his series “My Neck Is Thinner than a Hair: Engines,” but each lists the work with different dates (2000—03 and 1996—2004, respectively). And though Raad says he discontinued the Atlas Group in 2004, a work from the Group appears in the 2026 Venice Biennale catalog, with the date “printed 2023”—leaving it ambiguous as to when it was made, and whether the Group has really disbanded at all.

Still, one date is clear: Over the past two decades—since a 2005 catalyst—Raad’s work has only grown stranger. The Atlas Group primed viewers to read his documents as unstable, but the later work asks them to contend with shrunken objects, resurrected paintings, and vampires lurking in the archive. Something has shifted, and the old language of fact and fiction only scratches the surface.

IN A RESTORED 19th-century barn perched on a peak in the so-called “Irish Alps” in upstate New York, Raad keeps a meticulous archive. About an hour’s drive from Bard College, where he teaches, he and his wife duplicated the barn’s floor plan to build a second structure nearby: their home. The view from their porch is straight out of a Hudson River School painting, and meeting him for the first time feels like a peek behind the curtain: For over 20 years, he has diligently hidden his likeness from all corners of the internet, populating the algorithm with other faces to throw it off his scent. He explained his evasiveness in one word—“phobia”—but it was hard not to see it as just one more way Raad uses photography to make the world feel larger and stranger, rather than to try to “capture” it. In person, he is warm and welcoming, serving homemade tabbouleh and hummus “the right way”—with sumac and olive oil.

In the barn, Raad has assiduously organized ephemeral materials like wall labels from his exhibitions and name cards from dinners he’s attended, all fodder that may or may not become an artwork in the future. A strappy leather portfolio contained his juvenilia, including those pictures he made as a teenager. He went to high school in Boston—“They had a darkroom and they had a basketball team, so it was great,” he said—where he made pictures in the style of Cindy Sherman, Diane Arbus, Garry Winogrand, Stephen Shore, Henri Cartier-Bresson, and Lucas Samaras. Raad was able to approximate all of their styles, but what he carried from the exercise most clearly was the experience of embodying a persona from behind the camera.

In 1985, Raad started his undergraduate degree at the Rochester Institute of Technology, where he majored in medicine before switching to photography. While there, he won his first photography prize, for a work he made under the pseudonym P.X. Chesterfield, inspired by a real US Marine Corps general, P.X. Kelley, whose name he thought sounded cool. Soon after, he enrolled in the University of Rochester’s “Cultural and Visual Studies” PhD program, which sported rising-star faculty: Craig Owens, Kaja Silverman, Douglas Crimp. It “was psychoanalysis, linguistics, and Marxism,” Raad explained. “The holy trinity.” For Raad, persona, theory, and photography were starting to converge.

As a student, Raad visited and photographed Beirut each summer, a practice he continues to this day. Back home, he tried aping observational techniques from Diane Arbus or Eugène Atget that he’d observed in photography magazines his dad gave him. But he found that “even something as simple as using a tripod was impossible… in a city that’s full of snipers.” He wasn’t making war photography, either, never capturing the actions, always the aftermath.

After taking pictures of detonated bombs, however, Raad was often left with the sense that something was missing, so he started getting his hands on the pictures—circling detritus with a red pencil. Kernels of his most famous works are palpable in his teenage years, which seems appropriate for an artist who describes himself as starting out with an interest in “a certain way of thinking about violence and trauma.” Versions of those red circles recur in the Atlas Group’s Let’s Be Honest, the Weather Helped (1998/2006), black-and-white snapshots of Beirut marked with brightly colored dots corresponding to the code system that ammunition manufacturers use to identify cartridges and shells—and thus, indirectly, their makers. In Raad’s hands, the dots read as much confetti as forensic notations.

Under the Atlas Group, Raad was crafting personas like the gambling historian Dr. Fadl Fakhouri and the unlucky police detective Yussef Bitar—“very serious, very professional people,” he explained—the kind likely to leave behind official documents. But eventually, he found the Atlas Group “somewhat limited,” and became interested in showing how “violence has more insidious effects than we know.” Besides, he added, by the early aughts, he felt that “the language of maps and archives had been exhausted.”

RAAD’S THINKING BEGAN to shift after meeting, in the early ’90s, the Lebanese writer and artist Jalal Toufic while working on a video project about the occupation of South Lebanon. He started reading Toufic’s books, which he found difficult to parse at first, but eventually, he found Forthcoming (2000). That book includes the story of a classically trained photographer who can’t stop making blurry pictures of buildings in Beirut. Raad instantly recognized himself.

“I freaked out,” Raad told me. “It was as if he could hear my internal monologue.” He thought about how certain photographic tropes—something as simple as a tripod—had been rendered unavailable to him in wartime Beirut, but soon was thinking more expansively about all that violence had withdrawn from him. His trinity-training in Rochester had taught him that “language, psyche, the economy… that’s the stuff of the world.” Toufic, he said, gave him language for “a different place that I’d never been introduced to.”

Toufic has influenced almost everything Raad has made since that encounter. “I’m embarrassed by how much I talk about that guy,” he told me. “It’s as if I cannot have a thought without passing through him.” Of lasting impact was Toufic’s concept of “withdrawal,” spelled out most explicitly in The Withdrawal of Tradition Past a Surpassing Disaster (2009) but also addressed in earlier essays. In it, he describes the sorts of immaterial losses that can arise in the wake of major cultural upheavals—the ways that rituals and forms can become unavailable or lose their potency when the society that gave rise to them is changed irreversibly by disaster.

Tradition, Toufic theorizes, might be clung to steadfastly in the aftermath of disaster, as in the revival of Orthodox Judaism in the wake of the Holocaust; or it might be suppressed entirely, as in versions of modernism that, also in the wake of the world wars, try in vain to imagine a clean slate and abolish antecedents. When a tradition comes back to life in a new context, something is always off: Toufic calls the act a “resurrection,” because the tradition is not alive so much as undead. The artist’s job is to make this withdrawal palpable—to make the absence present, “like the mirror in vampire films”; for Toufic, only those who try and fail to resurrect withdrawn tradition “may become truly absolutely modern.”

This concept of withdrawal informed the pivotal work Raad showed at the Arab world’s first white cube gallery, Sfeir-Semler Gallery, which opened in 2005. He’d declined the invitation several times before eventually acquiescing in 2008, sensing that something seemed off. When he arrived at the gallery, he found that the Atlas Group’s work he shipped had been shrunk to 1/100th of its original size. When I pressed Raad on how this could be possible, he said that “there are conditions under which your own work is no longer available to you, and your only relation to it feels distorted.” For him, this is not “a symptom, and not a metaphor.” It’s also “not quantum,” nor a condition of “one’s psyche, material conditions, or language”—it is, he said, “withdrawal.” Withdrawal is also the very reason he could not complete those Arafat bed paintings.

The affinities between Raad and Toufic are striking enough that more than one person has confessed their suspicion that Toufic is simply another of Raad’s personas—a theory that would require an elaborate ruse if true, with Raad hiring a body double to appear alongside him at public events. But while Raad is undoubtedly skilled at crafting fictions and personas, he is less interested in pranks than in fables—in what happens when something is imagined as having been true rather than in trickery and illusion.

AFTER THE ATLAS GROUP mined the archive and rendered it strange, Raad’s work went beyond scrambling fact and fiction and toward something more like magical realism. Along the way, photography—which is so hard to read without thinking about truth—became less central. Better be watching the clouds again and again (2000/2017) is a series of collages attributed to a fictional Lebanese Army officer named Fadwa Hassoun, who’d trained as a botanist. During the war, Hassoun assigned politicians flowers as code names, and the work that tells her story features black-and-white portraits of Benjamin Netanyahu, Saddam Hussein, Ronald Reagan, and more with their heads crowned by colorful petals, their legs made to look like stems.

More recently, Raad collaborated with graphic designer Pierre Huyghebaert on I thought I’d escape my fate (again) (2025), an installation that gathers statements from people involved in exhibitions and programs canceled over expressions of solidarity with Palestine. Printed, cut out, and taped low along a gallery baseboard, these quotes are hard to read without crouching. What catches the eye instead are the colored strips of tape running across the wall, like placeholders for the artworks that never got to hang in such a space. It’s another example of how disaster can show up in art sideways, of Toufic’s idea that conflict leaves traces that are visible in artworks and cultural traditions only in the form of absence—that a “truly modern” artwork might make this absence visible.

Toufic’s vampire-mirror idea resurfaces too in other works of Raad’s on display in Venice, alongside the Arafat pieces. Copies of stolen Arab and Turkish artworks appear painted on the undersides of wooden pallets. Here, as in several recent works, the vampire Raad holds a mirror up to is modern Arab art itself, which lately has undergone a period of “rediscovery,” to use the art world’s favorite term—or, resurrection. When the Lebanese Civil War ended in 1990, a wall text informs, militias sold off weapons, many of which found their way to the Balkans; the Yugoslav Wars, then, were fought partly with Lebanese arms. The text adds that the painted pallets were recently found in Ljubljana, at the Moderna Galerija—where, conveniently, he just closed a mid-career retrospective.

Next spring, at Paula Cooper Gallery in New York, Raad will place a vintage VW Beetle on its back in the gallery like a dying bug—a reference to “flying Volkswagens,” as American soldiers called the artillery shells they fired on Beirut in the 1980s. Surrounding them on the walls will be reproductions of handwritten notes left on bombs by soldiers in various languages, including English, Russian, Arabic, Hebrew, and French—like xoxo, or the dildo of consequences rarely arrives lubed, or from silicon valley with love. Raad found images on Reddit posted by braggadocious soldiers from around the world, and then exaggerated the size and changed the color of their inscriptions. There isn’t a whole lot of fiction or fantasy in this one: Sometimes, the facts are strange enough.

item.title: Artists Take to the Streets Amid Massive Protests in France - Hyperallergic
item.description:
PARIS — On the heels of last Saturday’s mass protests — and amid the preemptive closure of Art Basel Paris and museums like the Louvre — Paris’s artists, culture workers, and art students were back in the streets today, October 24.

Tens of thousands gathered at Porte d’Italie for a march called in part by Cultures en Lutte, the network of culture-sector coalitions that has mobilized alongside the labor confederations and student unions since the movement began in mid-September, and by one of its driving forces, the National Union of Visual Artists (SNAP-CGT). 

They came despite a week of warnings. After the destruction of October 17, the French government announced a “massive” security deployment: Sentinelle anti-terror soldiers would relieve police of guard duties, while special units would be backed by helicopters, armored vehicles, and water cannons. More than 250,000 protestors turned out anyway in Paris, and several hundred thousand more around the country, reports estimate. Police arrested approximately 1,000 protesters just today.

item.title: In a Historic Blunder, Wu-Tang Clan Sold an Album as a Unique Artwork—A New Doc Tells the Story of an Architect of the Sale - ARTnews.com
item.description:
If you were on the internet in 2015, you likely followed the twisty tale of the Wu-Tang Clan’s Once Upon a Time in Shaolin. The Staten Island hip-hop titans conceived of the album as a conceptual artwork, a protest against the cheapening of music in the age of widespread piracy. Rather than release the music to the general public, the work was sold at auction for a reported $2 million to a then-anonymous American buyer, seemingly proving that music could sell at the level of Picasso and Warhol.

It proved a Pyrrhic victory when the buyer was revealed to be the hated “pharma bro” Martin Shkreli. The episode was a bitter lesson for the group, resulting in resentment and division. Even Clan member Method Man said, “Fuck that album. … When music can’t be music and y’all turning it into something else, fuck that. Give it to the people, if they want to hear the shit, let them have it. Give it away free.” (He somewhat softened his stance recently, on finally hearing the album.)

A new Netflix documentary, The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable (2026), presents a long and shaggy ride through the experience. Directed by producer Joanna Natasegara and featuring RZA as an executive producer, the film proves a frustrating watch: no one involved seems to, even now, have thought much about the lessons from their attempt to hijack the art market, a sometimes unpredictable world they blundered into, seeming to know little about it while somehow assuming that’s where the big money was. “Contemporary art is worth millions by virtue of its exclusivity,” said the band at the time. Of course, a vanishingly small percentage of artworks of any era are priced at that level, but maybe their misconception is understandable, since the members’ art world reference points, at least judging by the way they are quoted in the film, seem to be restricted to Leonardo da Vinci, Picasso, and Warhol.

Many of the art world’s denizens could have warned them away from the stunt. Funnily enough, in 2017, during the whole dustup, Richard Prince disavowed an artwork he had sold to Ivanka Trump before her father’s entry into politics. Of course, by then it was too late to warn RZA.

The album’s sale is mentioned in the opening sequence, with audio of an unidentified interviewer calling it “one of the coolest stories in art history.” RZA explains the thinking: “We’ll make one single copy of the album, treat it like it’s the Mona Lisa. It was a combination of ideas that led to it. Me and my student Cilvaringz—won’t take all the credit.”

“Would you ever do it again?” asks the interviewer.

Says the rapper, in a loaded two-letter word, “Um …”

The Shaggy Tale of an Unfolding Mess

The film then doesn’t mention the album again for a full 55 minutes, instead plunging the viewer at great length into the life story of Dutch-Moroccan rapper-producer Tarik Azzougarh, one of the masterminds of the project, including his traumatic childhood experiences of racism and abuse.

The director found him compelling, she explains in press materials: “Over a long lunch in beautiful Marrakech, where he lived, Tarik told me the twists and turns of the album’s 30-year story, and I was fascinated. It wasn’t only a great story; it resonated with me personally as someone who grew up in the ’90s with mixed heritage. The Wu-Tang Clan often talk about being teenagers inspired by East Asian culture through movies, while Tarik and his friends had, in turn, been inspired by the Clan.”

Unfortunately, for my money, Azzougarh doesn’t ultimately prove a compelling presence on screen. “I figured that a doc would show my side of the story,” Azzougarh tells the off-camera director early on, in a characteristically not-quite-electrifying observation.

The film slowly relates that the aspiring rapper and superfan ingratiated himself into the band’s circles, flying to New York multiple times as a teenager for the purpose. He earned the sobriquet Cilvaringz and membership in the Killa Beez, a network of musicians in the extended Wu-Tang family, releasing his own records on their imprint as well as producing some of the Clan’s albums.

Once Upon a Time was packaged in a custom handcrafted silver box and traveled with all the pomp and security of a seven-figure artwork, as the film shows. Only one copy will ever legally exist, in a protest against the loss of music’s aura in the age of its digital reproducibility, to paraphrase German philosopher Walter Benjamin. The band sold the record via online auctioneer Paddle8 in 2015, with the stipulation that the buyer could not release it commercially for 88 years, though they could play it at listening parties.

In keeping with the fine art theme, the band staged a listening event at MoMA PS1, after which Complex described the record as “rich, layered, and sonically bombastic,” with a “rugged, hard-hitting sound” reminiscent of early Wu-Tang Clan albums. Writing for ARTnews, a slightly more skeptical Dan Duray noted, “There were plenty of unexpected samples, melodramatic horns, cheesy bits of kung-fu dialogue.” Snippets are audible in the documentary.

Then Shkreli was arrested, and some of the film’s funnier moments come with the discussion of Wu-Tang’s attempts to find a way to reverse the sale and get the music to the people, including a rumored clause in the contract by which either Clan members or actor Bill Murray could legally steal the record back.

In 2018, Shkreli was convicted of securities fraud and conspiracy, and the Department of Justice sold the record to help pay his reparations. In 2021, it sold, for some $4 million, to digital art and crypto collective PleasrDAO, in whose hands it remains today. The group’s late founder, Jamis Johnson, said in 2021 that “there’s not a world in which we don’t own this album.” The group has organized several listening events, at venues from the Museum of Old and New Art in Tasmania to the Angel Orensanz Center, housed in a 175-year-old former synagogue in New York.

So now Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, with all its contradictions and challenges, is PleasrDAO’s problem. In a video interview with ARTnews, the collective’s “chief pleasing officer,” Jamis’s brother Adrian Johnson, outlined the tricky position in which the group finds itself.

“We don’t want the record to be streamed,” he said. “The moment it is, it becomes another album.”

He went on, “Everything about it is a paradox: it’s for the people, but it’s also highly guarded. It’s quite a difficult job as stewards of this art to say, ‘How can we bring it to the people but not devalue it?,’ and I don’t believe that keeping it locked away is right. I also don’t believe making it freely available is right. So we are constantly looking for creative ways to share this with the people.”

For future activations, keep an eye on a dedicated website, and tune in to Netflix for the documentary, but don’t hold out for too much excitement. I give it a passing grade.

item.title: Portrait of a Paris Art Week on Fire - Hyperallergic
item.description:
PARIS — “The people in the art world are courageous,” a collector told me at Asia Now, the first of the Paris art fairs that opened early in the week on Monday, in the heat of the protests. “But I would still like to be back at my hotel before 7pm, you know, just in case.”

Anyone who is a regular at Paris Art Week has a collection of stories about something going wrong. In 2022, there were strikes and cost-of-living marches. In October 2023, France was on high terror alert, and one of the bomb threats that emptied the airports of the country’s major cities led to, among other things, my plane landing in the middle of the French countryside. A couple of trains later, and voilà: I was in Paris in time for the vernissages.

This time, when I rolled my suitcase out of the Gare du Nord station late on the afternoon of Saturday, October 17, I was prepared. I breathed in the crisp air and smelled the burning plastic and walked past the black-clad protesters running from squads of police while firefighters put out scattered fires. I was supposed to meet a friend who lives in the Marais later that evening, but she couldn’t get home. She had planned a quiet, aesthetic weekend with her family to see shows and the art fair; she had even planned her outfits. What she found instead on Boulevard de Sébastopol, at the edge of her neighborhood, was the police playing cat and mouse with protesters.

“We had to run!” she told me. “When the police start hitting, they hit indiscriminately.” She had just come back from the Portuguese city of Porto, where local officers charged a peaceful housing-rights camp at 3 am, while people were still half asleep in their tents.

Around 11pm, she and her family finally made it home, closed the door behind them, and breathed a sigh of relief.

Ready for Art Week?

The Eve of Destruction

“I think the art fairs, in this context, are rather grotesque,” tells me French-Moroccan artist El Mehdi Largo, who is skipping them all this year. “Then again, art fairs are pretty grotesque in any context.”

We are sitting in a café on rue Poissonnière, with a view of smashed glass and clusters of burned bikes that looked like the melted surfaces of Alberto Burri’s Combustioni.

Largo continued, noting that while art wouldn’t exist without the bourgeoisie and the rich patrons of the Renaissance, in today’s art world and economy, what really matters is taxes and how to move money around: “For the elites, it could be art, or it could be thoroughbred horses; it won’t make any difference!”

It was the day after the clashes on Saturday, and there is still excitement, bewilderment, and disarray in the air, the kind you feel when something is about to change. Everybody was filming the destruction, and you couldn’t sit next to a group of people, or walk past one, without hearing about the protests. “I’m flabbergasted.” “Have you seen what went down in Marseille?”

In the heat of the revolt, small shops were not spared, but the majority of the windows I saw destroyed belonged to Carrefour supermarkets, banks, real estate agencies, luxury brands, and government buildings.

And of course, there was the looting. “It’s quite shocking,” said a Lebanese friend who moved to Paris to escape the bombing of Beirut, and whose daughter is among the students marching. “In Lebanon, people were so hungry, but they still have their dignity; they would never loot.” She paused. “Here, people are really, really angry.”

Le peuple, the people, are a Dionysian force, made up of individuals with different motives, agendas, and energies, with different responses to oppression and repression. Over the past few days, a protest this widespread has had a bit of everything, from those taking food and tampons for the homeless to the kids who are just smashing windows. It’s a gradient.

The mix is in the people and in the writing on the walls. On a street corner, a handwritten cardboard sign propped up among the bird control spikes quotes the French philosopher Simone Weil: “Il est donné à très peu d’esprits de découvrir que les choses et les êtres existent.” (“Very few minds discover that things and beings exist.”) A few blocks away, the message is more straightforward: “Nique la police,” “fuck the police.”

An Italian curator who lives in Paris spent that Saturday in the Marais setting up her show, which opened on Sunday. “I pulled down the shutters, and it was surreal to put up the works when outside there was basically a civil war!” People banged on the iron doors; she heard running and screaming outside, and tear gas seeped in.

Her unbothered French boyfriend, clearly used to the Shiva dance on the French people, reassured her: “Nothing to worry about, chérie, protests are always like this here!”

Back to Business

Across town, the Grand Palais had gone through its own lockdown. At 5pm on Saturday, while galleries were installing Art Basel Paris, the police prefecture ordered a lockdown of the building, and for a while nobody could get in or get out. It reopened the next day without a scratch.

Around it, the cultural calendar was struggling to hold up. On October 15, the Foreign Ministry had already postponed a design show by Thierry Lemaire and Harry Nuriev in the salons of the Quai d’Orsay, judging it ill-timed given the social climate. Its title: PASSAGES. Pas sages, a French pun on “disobedient.”

On Sunday, the Jeu de Paume called off the VIP opening of its Stan Douglas show. On Monday, students from the École du Louvre blocked the entrance of the Louvre museum, and that evening, students forced the École des Beaux-Arts to cancel its Gina Pane opening.

The interior minister acknowledged that the police had “lost control” over the weekend. The Chinese, German, and United States embassies told citizens to stay away from protest areas, and an overnight curfew, from 11 pm to 6 am, was imposed on Place de la République and part of Les Halles, on either side of the Marais.

By Tuesday afternoon, when Art Basel’s ultra-VIP “Avant-Première” — a preview of the preview — opened, the Grand Palais was ringed with concrete anti-ram barriers, and police and private security patrol around the clock. Inside, the fair went on, business as usual; no one was talking about the protests anymore.

“I bet no one is talking about them!” exclaimed one of my editors, whom I caught frantically typing in a corridor of the Grand Palais. “They’re too busy selling works for millions of dollars!”

By Wednesday, the streets around the Grand Palais, largely spared, have been cleaned up. The burned cars and gutted shops are further east, around Bastille and République, safely out of sight, and cleaning crews are all over the city, painting over the graffiti and repairing shattered windows.

Collector Selim Bouafsoun had come for the Avant-Première, already bought a few pieces, and saw nothing of the protests beyond the debris of the breakages. Inside the Grand Palais, “it felt safe and like a good environment to do business.”

“I come from Tunisia,” he told me. “We do not get scared by manifestations. Manifestations are a right, and we respect their rights.”

Outside, on Avenue Winston Churchill, Alicja Kwade’s “L’Élévation des Mondes” (2026), a 14-foot stack of stone spheres that her gallery described as evoking the Tower of Babel and the failure of universal systems of order, came down on Friday instead of Sunday, among other works removed ahead of the weekend protests. On Instagram, Kwade wrote, “Protest is good, but why everything has to be smashed and destroyed is beyond ……It certainly doesn't help the cause.”

An Incredible Happening

On Thursday afternoon, I’m at Offscreen, the fair held in the Chapelle Saint-Louis de la Salpêtrière, when an email from Art Basel lands in my inbox: The fair will close on Friday at 7 pm, two days early, “in the interest of safeguarding our visitors” ahead of the weekend protests.

“In any case, the sales have already been made, so the business is done,” noted Marina Vinogradova, director of NIKA Project Space in Dubai. The gallery represents Iraqi-Finnish Adel Abidin, whom I had come to interview at Offscreen.

We sit on a bench in front of the chapel of the old Salpêtrière hospital, where Paris once confined its mentally ill. Our conversation about what painting means in today’s world is interrupted by helicopters and sirens. A long line of police vans pulls up in the street just outside, and armed officers take position.

I ask Abidin how it feels to participate in an art fair in such a context. “While I condemn the vandalism and the violence, I think it’s inspiring to see that people can protest and have a voice,” he told me. “I wish I’d had that when I was living in Baghdad.” He doesn’t think art is useless at a moment like this. “Art, like every other gesture, is part of something bigger. Making art, like protesting, is a way of challenging what’s happening. They’re not really opposites.” 

He laughs. “I know I might sound naive or idealistic, but I do believe that change comes from the sum of all these gestures.”

This kind of attitude is not necessarily shared by everyone. Thursday at lunchtime, I meet one last time with El Mehdi Largo in my neighborhood, the 9th Arrondissement.

“They instrumentalize our suffering,” he said. “I’m sure at the fairs you have seen plenty of works dealing with social issues. In the end, they’re only there to decorate. To decorate the conversations of the people who can afford them: ‘Look what I found, look at my sensibility.’”

“Honestly, I’m still hopeful there’ll be some smashing. For me, it would be the ultimate art form, an incredible happening: les casseurs walking into the Grand Palais, or in any of these art temples.” 

He stopped for a second, then added: “But then, of course, this will become the aesthetic of smashing. Damn. There is no way out, isn’t it?”

item.title: How Art Can Deliver Justice for Refugees - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Enayet Khan fled Myanmar in 2017. For three days, he moved through forests and fields with his family, slipping from one village to the next as fires closed in behind them. Each time they stopped, the safety was temporary — by morning, that village too would be burning. His own home had already been reduced to ash, but there was no time to mourn what was lost. Armed soldiers moved quickly, and Khan saw people being shot in front of him. The goal was simple : to survive long enough to find a way out of Myanmar. Ten members of his family fled together; three were injured along the way. Eventually, they crossed the border into Bangladesh.

“I lost everything,” Khan told Hyperallergic in a phone call. “Home, documentation, property, a sense of security.”

Khan settled in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, now home to nearly one million Rohingya refugees. The Rohingya people have endured decades of discrimination and repression under Myanmar’s successive governments. Stripped of citizenship by a 1982 law, they remain one of the largest stateless groups in the world. Most fled in 2017 to escape the military’s crimes against humanity and genocide.

In the camps, Khan turned to painting and drawing to process the atrocities he had witnessed: burning homes, fleeing families, and executions. Over time, he began training other refugees to do the same, establishing the Rohingya Art Club (RAC) and encouraging visual storytelling as a form of expression and resistance.

Khan is one of many refugees using art to record experiences of conflict and violence. According to legal experts, such work can also play a role in accountability efforts, helping to convey testimony and corroborate survivor accounts, and even enter legal proceedings as evidence of mass atrocities.

A record 117.8 million people have been forcibly displaced worldwide — a number that has risen for 12 consecutive years. Investigations and prosecutions of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes have surged within the European Union, with new cases increasing by 44% between 2016 and 2021. Today, more displaced people are turning to international courts to hold perpetrators accountable, an increase in demand that the International Criminal Court (ICC) itself has called “unprecedented.”

For some legal advocates, art has become one way to meet that demand.

Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide and a former United Nations investigator, collected artwork as part of the evidence in a case before the International Court of Justice that charged the Myanmar military with genocide against Rohingya communities in 2017. She noted that the high illiteracy rate among Rohingya people, especially women and children, makes it difficult to record traditional statements. In those contexts, drawings became a vital way to convey their testimonies.

item.title: The War on Art Is Repeating Itself - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Critic and theater director Isaac Butler is younger than I am, so he didn’t live through the Culture Wars of the Reagan ’80s. During this time, for instance, the Morality Action Committee wrote postcards to legislators across the country claiming that Franklin Furnace — the arts organization I founded 50 years ago — had shown pornography to 500 children per day during our Carnival Knowledge exhibition of women artists exploring sexuality. But as an art aficionado, he saw an alarming development in 2020, when an exhibition of Philip Guston’s work was postponed by the Tate Modern; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; and the National Gallery of Art for fear that his paintings referencing the Ku Klux Klan might be misinterpreted by the public. In light of the current rise of right-wing legislators, politicians, and organizations targeting arts and culture in the United States, the parallel story of the conservative players of the 1980s and ’90s needs to be told. 

Butler’s book, The Perfect Moment: God, Sex, Art, and the Birth of America's Culture Wars (2026), discusses major events in that tumultuous era of the 1980s and ’90s, including the difficulty Martin Scorsese had producing The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), primarily caused by Reverend Donald Wildmon’s innovation of mass mailing to Christians on behalf of his National Federation for Decency. Wildmon appears again in Butler’s discussion of Andres Serrano’s infamous “Piss Christ” (1987), a photograph of a plastic crucifix in a beaker of the artist’s urine. In 1989, then-Senator Alfonse D’Amato ripped a reproduction of a catalog image of Serrano’s artwork in half on the Senate floor.

Then there’s the story that gives the book its name: the cancellation of The Perfect Moment, a Robert Mapplethorpe retrospective, by the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. By the mid-1980s, Mapplethorpe’s AIDS diagnosis had become common knowledge. Although The Perfect Moment had traveled nationally, its depiction of sadomasochism, Black nude models, and naked children was likely going to get a reaction in Washington. So on June 12, 1989, the Corcoran Gallery of Art decided to cancel the exhibition before it opened, after which Jesse Helms and Sidney Yates, a Democratic Congressman from Illinois, fought over the funding of the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) itself. Butler provides a balanced account of how both sides strategized and implemented their ambitions.

item.title: The Center Cannot Hold at the Toronto Biennial - Hyperallergic
item.description:
TORONTO — At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared that the world is “in the midst of a rupture, not a transition.” The line is quoted in the catalog for the fourth Toronto Biennial of Art, Things Fall Apart, and could serve as the exhibition’s epigraph.

Curated by Allison Glenn, who spent her childhood in Detroit, crossing into Canada through Windsor, the edition brings together more than 30 artists and collectives across Toronto and, for the first time, sites beyond it, including Anchorage in Alaska and Times Square in New York.

Glenn keeps the Biennial’s long-running focus on water, taking the Great Lakes as her point of departure to ask what artists who work with rupture can teach us about histories, borders, and movement. With Canada–United States relations at an unprecedented low, a cross-border exhibition built around shared waterways feels just right.

The most affecting works treat histories of rupture as an imaginative encounter to be conjured rather than a settled narrative to be recorded. At the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), Dawoud Bey’s Material Histories, Living Landscapes hangs photographs from three landscape series tightly together around his two-channel video “350,000” (2023), alongside sculptures and ritual objects from the AGO’s collection with roots in Nigeria, Ghana, and the Kingdom of Kongo. The pairing sets up a striking sonic and visual call and response across the Middle Passage, elucidating the ways the afterlife of slavery permeates the physical world around us. The film’s point-of-view movement through dense woods, accompanied by the sound of heavy breathing and black-and-white images of gnarled landscapes and old homes, suggests that the fight to live free from racial violence is still an urgent one today.  

At the University of Toronto Art Centre, the exhibition’s main venue, Antonio Obá strings rows of brass bells across the length of a gallery for “Jardim” (2022–26), which visitors brush against as they walk a processional path. The work sounds only when bodies move through it; memory here is repeatedly reperformed rather than stored as an unchanging artifact. The path leads to “A Folia: travessia” (The Revelry: A Crossing, 2026), a large painting that reimagines Douglas Martin’s 1957 photograph of 15-year-old Dorothy Counts integrating a high school in Charlotte, North Carolina. Obá replaces the crowd that jeered and spat at her with one resembling both a supportive march and a New Orleans-style street carnival, a striking intervention within a painful chapter in history that points us toward a restorative alternate reality. He's asking us to imagine being there with Dorothy in that moment, surrounding her with courage and love; to let go of fear and hatred; to march toward and for a better future.

Moving from the historical to the personal, a second group of works takes knowledge held in bodies, materials, and practice as its guide. Wen Liu’s “In Light, Where Edges Yield” (2025), a human-scale steel-and-resin sculpture built around a spinal column, suspends Chinese herbal medicines prescribed to the artist after her father’s death, the herbs glowing like stained glass. It suggests that the body acts as an important source of familial and personal knowledge that might both illuminate our experience and carry us through difficult, disruptive periods.  

Taqralik Partridge’s “umiakkut (by boat)” (2026) revisits the journey her grandmother and siblings made across the Hudson Strait in a umiaq boat used by Indigenous Arctic peoples. In a mirrored room, she conjures the vessel, usually made with animal skins, from found materials, sewing, and beadwork, while an elder relative’s voice drifts through a soundtrack of water, passing on intergenerational knowledge that serves as a guide in this time of ecological devastation. 

Two standout works use place to reunite what was once separated. At the Royal Ontario Museum, Raphaël Barontini fills the Crystal Court with massive, draped textile panels that fold images of masks and sacred objects from the museum’s collections into an allegory of the Americas. “Follow the North Star – a Tribute to Harriet Tubman” (2026) connects Caribbean aesthetics that include anti-slavery heroines, water gods, and mythical figures to the Underground Railroad, a secret network that guided Black freedom seekers out of American slavery to a Canadian freedom still marred by racism. It casts liberation as a collective struggle that transcends not only geographic borders but the divide between the physical and spiritual. 

Meanwhile, in the nearby town of Scarborough, Nirbhai (nep) Singh Sidhu’s “A Deathless Potential In Remembrance By You” (2026), a permanent structure at the Scarborough Gurdwara built with earth from Sirhind, Punjab, is made for simran, the Sikh practice of stillness and deep listening. Bricks, steel, and water come together, binding paths of spiritual awakening to survival.

A final highlight, Rouzbeh Akhbari’s “Of Wool and Diesel” (2026) at Mercer Union, moves from these embodied and spiritual paths to geopolitical and economic ones. The 30-minute film follows the informal sheep trade around the Strait of Hormuz, binding shepherds and flocks to smugglers and moneychangers. Made as war in Iran was shutting down trade routes, it refuses to treat rupture as enclosure. Borders close, routes collapse, yet people and exchange persist.

Spread across more than 13 Toronto sites, with plenty of programming still to come, Things Fall Apart is ambitious and timely. It's a provocative and discursive exploration of how artists respond to our late-capitalist epoch with works that adapt to its social, political, and ecological realities rather than mourn what has broken. One challenge, though, is cohesion. The physical distance between sites and the dizzying range of subjects, from Inuit migration to Gulf smuggling, make it hard to hold as a whole.

But the deeper problem lies in the exhibition’s foundational concept. Rupture, as Carney and others envision it, presupposes a prior unity, and the exhibition never satisfactorily examines or troubles that perceived unity. Glenn’s catalog essay raises the right question (rupture to what, and by whom?), but the exhibition seldom pursues it with rigor. As I encountered each work, I repeatedly felt myself asking: Was there a time since modernity — which is inextricably tied to slavery, colonial extraction, empire, forced migration, genocide — when the so-called world order did not feel ruinous to those on its underside? The rupture may be less new than newly felt by those who have sought to order the world to their liking.

Things Fall Apart, the fourth iteration of the Toronto Biennial of Art, continues at venues across Toronto as well as select sites elsewhere through December 20. The exhibition was curated by Allison Glenn.

item.title: Artist Duo Brognon Rollin Awarded 2026 Prix Marcel Duchamp, France’s Top Art Prize - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Prix Marcel Duchamp jury announced Thursday that it has awarded the 2026 prize to artist duo David Brognon and Stéphanie Rollin, known for their multidisciplinary practice that spans installation, sculpture, video, performance, and photography.

The Prix Marcel Duchamp is considered France’s most prestigious art prize, with winners recieving €35,000, or just over $40,000. For the award, a jury typically selects four nominees, who show together at the Centre Pompidou in October. This year, however, five nominees were chosen—Malagasy artist Joël Andrianomearisoa, Josèfa Ntjam, a participant in last year’s Bienal de São Paulo, artist and filmmaker Laura Henno, and Brognon and Rollin—and the annual exhibition was held at Musée d’Arte Moderne de Paris due to the Pompidou’s extended closure.

This year’s jury comprised Xavier Rey, director of the Centre Pompidou, along with Claude Bonnin, director of Adiaf, the organization that has facilitated the prize since its creation in 2000; Akemi Shiraha, of the Association Marcel Duchamp; Fabrice Hergott, director of the Musée d’Art Moderne; collectors Fernando Arriola and Marie-Cécile Zinsou; artists Kader Attia (who himself won the Prix Marcel Duchamp in 2016) and Berlinde de Bruyckere; Karin Hindsbo, director of the Tate Modern; and Christophe Leribault, president of the Château de Versailles.

For the exhibition at MAM, Brognon Rollin presented the exhibition 5,376 years, 1,892 months, 1,110 days, 1,201 hours, which consisted of coin-pusher machines filled with sobriety tokens like those given to members of Alcoholics Anonymous when they achieve certain sobriety milestones.

“With Brognon Rollin, the Prix Marcel Duchamp recognises a demanding body of work that gives tangible form to what usually escapes our gaze: the passage of time spent waiting, addiction and inner resilience,” said Fabrice Hergott, director of the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, in a statement. “The work they have created for the museum, presenting these fairground objects through a subtle installation, fundamentally shifts our perspective. It is a quiet yet tenacious statement on human vulnerability and the exploration of our inner lives.

In addition to the €35,000 awarded to the winner, ADIAF, the prize’s sponsor, provides an additional €40,000 in financial support to the nominees and their galleries, as well as a feature in a dedicated annual publication.

The Prix Marcel Duchamp exhibition will remain on view at MAM through February 7, 2027. It has been curated by Odile Burluraux, chief curator at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, and Nicolas Liucci-Goutnikov, curator at the Centre Pompidou—Musée national d’art
moderne and head of the Bibliothèque Kandinsky.

item.title: Scientists Contest Dating of Van Gogh’s "The Starry Night" - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Scholars have long accepted June 1889 as the month when Vincent van Gogh painted the iconic blue eddied-sky and idyllic hillside village of "The Starry Night." Yet a new Scientific Reports study published Thursday, October 22, calls for reconsidering that date, suggesting the Post-Impressionist painter may have drawn inspiration from a night sky that appeared a month later.

South Korean researchers Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, Suna Kang, Jungwoo Song, and Ho Jin argue that several celestial forms in the painting contradict the original June 1889 date and are better supported by the conditions of July that same year. The study incorporates tools that analyze star patterns and positions, contemporary weather models, van Gogh's letters, and other methods of inquiry in what the researchers call a "multidisciplinary framework."

"Earlier astronomical readings, constrained by the conventional June dating, reached mutually exclusive conclusions, and the painting’s celestial arrangement was never quantitatively tested," the report's abstract reads. "These findings suggest that the night sky in The Starry Night originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating."

In June 1889, the artist was weeks into his harrowing yearlong confinement at a French asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, a few months after he'd famously severed his left ear during a row with painter Paul Gauguin. The view from his asylum window was thought to have inspired his expressionist masterpiece, which is in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan.

item.title: ‘Street Photography Africa’ is a Colorful and Energetic Survey Across the Continent - Colossal
item.description:
From the markets of Dakar and Lagos to the sidewalks of Abidjan and the Beherawi neighborhood of Addis Abab, a bold new book by Nadine Barth and Azu Nwagbogu travels from country to country to present a vast portrait of life on the continent. Street Photography Africa compiles hundreds of images from 33 photographers who each turn their lens to public spaces, documenting cultural moments with musicians and dancers alongside more everyday fashions and routines. While vast in scope, location, and style, the nearly 300-page survey is connected by the central premise that “the street becomes a stage.”

Street Photography Africa is out this month from Thames & Hudson. Find your copy on Bookshop.

item.title: How Did ‘American Gothic’ Become So Iconic? This Art Historian Spent Five Decades Investigating. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In need of a couple’s costume this Halloween? Try a calico apron over a dark dress, a low bun with one loose strand, a cameo broach at your throat; dress a partner in overalls and wire-rimmed glasses, holding a three-pronged pitchfork. It won’t take much to be immediately recognizable as the duo from American Gothic, Grant Wood’s 1930 painting and subject of Wanda Corn’s new book, The Couple with the Pitchfork: American Gothic from Easel to Icon. Why, Corn wants to know, did this painting become so iconic?

Corn, an eminent scholar of American art, has been thinking about this question for five decades. The painting intersected with her own trajectory as an art historian and with her personal history as a descendent of the Midwest: the book includes a photograph of her grandparents posed side-by-side at their home in Indiana, her grandfather in denim overalls, and her grandmother with hair pulled back and a homemade dress. The parallels between the family photograph and American Gothic show how thoroughly Wood, himself raised in Iowa, was tapping in to regional Midwestern identity. Yet a portrait of a midwestern couple is hardly a promising candidate for global fame.

Of course, the pair in American Gothic aren’t a couple, at least not in Wood’s view. He claimed to have intended the twosome to represent a small-town father and daughter, basing the figures on his sister Nan and his dentist. When he made the painting, Wood was searching for a way of working that would be distinctive to the Midwest. He’d tried his hand at French Impressionism, taking several trips to Paris, and worked as a decorator back home in Cedar Rapids. Growing support for the arts in small town America, funded by philanthropists including the Carnegie Foundation, created more opportunities for Wood to make work that felt characteristic of his region.

American Gothic marked Wood’s embrace of a new style as an Iowa painter, developing a pictorial language suited to the visual culture of the Midwest. Rather than straightforward realism, Corn shows American Gothic to be the product of a thorough engagement with pattern and form. Vertical lines, from the tines of the pitchfork to the church steeple in the background, organize and order the composition. Round and oval forms—the figures’ long faces, the woman’s brooch, the pattern on the calico, the shape of the man’s ears—create harmony within the scene. Wood identified what he called a “decorative” quality in his subject matter, basic geometries and hard lines that he translated into paint with such precision that the work was taken to be self-evident rather than deeply thought.

The painting was immediately misunderstood. After winning a prize in a juried exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago, American Gothic—which reproduced well in newsprint thanks to those straightforward, geometric forms—became a sensation. Labeled by the press as a farmer and his wife, the depiction of the couple found detractors in both Iowans and art critics. Locals saw the pitchfork as outdated—four tines would have been more appropriate—and the woman unforgivably dour. Critics couldn’t place the work, finding it out of step with modernist abstraction. Everyone agreed it was an image of marriage.

For Corn, this misunderstanding is key to the painting’s success, allowing for endless adaptation of the archetypal form of two figures joined in union. She traces the painting’s influence in both art and popular culture, drawing on a personal archive of hundreds of reappropriations of the work: American Gothics in butter at a state fair, gay American Gothics in support of same-sex marriage, feminist American Gothics showing the woman heading off to work. Surprisingly, for a painting often dismissed as conservative and reactionary, some of the first adopters of its form were Black urban artists who saw the painting in Chicago in the 1930s. (The Art Institute acquired the painting soon after it debuted.) Certain African American artists saw in Wood a model for a self-taught artist from farm country. Reproducing the motif of a couple posed before a family home became a way of telling stories about migration for artists like Walter Ellison.

Corn’s explanation for American Gothic’s popularity is that it shows the archetype of marriage, a motif that can be traced from Egyptian princes to Etruscan terra cottas to Dutch golden age portraits, rendered in an accessible manner for the modern era. Yet unlike those other examples, beneath the smooth surface of Wood’s painting is a felt unease, a tension that animates the painting and motivates its adaptation. Wood, likely gay, experienced his own failed marriage five years after painting American Gothic. If his aesthetic was one of plainspoken values, he was also singularly able to capture all that goes unsaid when, as is so often the case, reality strains against the expectations of form.

item.title: Louvre Heist Suspect Denied Release As Investigators Unravel Tangled Testimonies - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An alleged member of the four-person team that broke into the Louvre last October, stealing crown jewels worth roughly $100 million, has been denied release, Le Figaro reports. The suspect, Rachid H., 40, has been detained since November 2025, and will remain in pre-trial detention, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled Wednesday.

On the morning of Sunday, October 19, 2025, the gang used a truck-mounted motorized ladder to break into the Louvre’s Apollo Gallery through a second-floor window. Once inside, they smashed two display cases and grabbed eight pieces of jewelry. (A crown once owned by Empress Eugénie was dropped in their haste.) As alarms sounded, they fled and escaped on two motorized scooters. The entire heist unfolded in roughly seven minutes.

The stolen jewels have yet to be recovered, but police have made relatively more in identifying the thieves. The first two suspects were arrested within a month of the heist: Abdoulaye N., 40, an unlicensed taxi driver with prior robbery convictions who is known online for his motocross stunts, and Ghelamallah A., 36, an unemployed Algerian national. Both have admitted involvement, though their testimony has raised more questions than it has answered.

In June, the two told investigators that a sponsor, whom they declined to name, had recruited them for the heist. They claimed to have been brought on just days before October 19, and the principal accomplice who gave them the orders, they said, remains at large, while the men arrested after them—including Rachid H.—had nothing to do with the crime. The purported mastermind, they claimed, had entered the Louvre with the robbers and remains at large.

Rachid H. was detained on suspicion of having provided the robbers with the keys to the parking facility in Aubervilliers. In January, AFP reported that he admitted to having “passed” the keys to “two people” but maintained that he knew nothing about the robbery. His defense has pointed out that his client’s fingerprints were found neither on the truck used in the heist nor in the parking lot where the robbers allegedly handed the jewels to an unidentified individual.

item.title: When Does a Woman Artist Reach Her "Prime"? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“What is an ‘old-age style’? Is it the same as a ‘late style’?” asks Linda Nochlin at the start of her 2008 essay, “Old-Age Style: Late Louise Bourgeois.” As our understanding of an artwork evolves with the artist’s age, the essay examines Bourgeois’s enduring aesthetics and interests throughout her seven-decade career, focusing particularly on the soft and hard qualities of her work. Nochlin, the esteemed feminist art historian, meditates on the relationship between a work made early in an artist’s career and one made at the end of their life, asking how the latter changes our understanding or interpretation of the former. Borrowing from the late Palestinian-American literary theorist Edward Said, Nochlin concludes that “late styles abandon all the comforting segues and aesthetic connections that hold the art object together, dealing instead with disconnects, abysses, unyielding dislocation and unresolved contradiction.” Late styles, in other words, force us to contend with shifts and disruptions in artistic focus, whether tied to an artist’s biography or not, that don’t fit neatly into historical assessments of earlier work. 

Nochlin’s definition of “late style” is helpful in understanding The Prime of Your Life, on view at Marc Straus Gallery in New York. Gathering 18 women artists over the age of 75, the exhibition is a cacophony of materials, concerns, and, yes, styles. Painting, drawing, sculpture, and installation, in wildly different scales, forms, and techniques, all congregate as a series of calls and responses rather than unified harmony. With only their age assembling them, the works in this exhibition offer less of a generational statement and more a critical question of 21st-century feminist art history: What does “prime” mean for a woman artist, when their work is most likely to be valorized by the market and museums only in their older age? 

Marina Abramović’s photograph “Standing with Skeleton” (2008/2016) introduces this question. Installed near the gallery’s entrance, the large-scale image depicts Abramović in black against an equally inky background with an ivory skeleton atop her back. Over 50 years, she has almost always used her body in her performance-driven work, eschewing subtlety for straight-on confrontation. She did this poetically with her 2010 epic performance and exhibition The Artist is Present, regarded as a career zenith, in which she stared opposite another individual during museum hours. Compared with the rigor and passion of Abramović's live performances, this photograph feels, at best, inanimate, and at worst, almost like a parody of her practice; the skeleton seems more like lighthearted Halloween decor than an elegiac meditation on old age. Does knowing the strength of Abramović's other work make this look like a comic pastiche? Is it fair to compare? Does a lesser, later work diminish the strength of the stronger, more provocative and innovative earlier one? How will we know if "Standing with Skeleton" is a late work? Perhaps now, at 79, Abramović is just hitting her prime, an epoch of work on the horizon.

item.title: Monet Painting Sells for $56.2 M., Setting French Auction Record at Sotheby’s Paris - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A Claude Monet painting sold for €50 million ($56.2 million) at Sotheby’s in Paris on Thursday, setting a record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.

The painting, Iris, sparked a 45-minute bidding battle between six collectors before selling to a private buyer in Asia, represented on the phone by Sotheby’s deputy chairman Jen Hua. It had been expected to fetch between €22 million and €30 million.

The sale was part of an auction of works from the collection of Jeanne Schlumberger, whose family made its fortune in the oil services industry. Every lot found a buyer, bringing the evening’s total to €74.4 million ($83.7 million), the highest ever for a fine art auction at Sotheby’s Paris. Nearly three-quarters of the lots sold above their high estimates.

Monet was responsible for most of the evening’s fireworks. A second painting, Saule pleureur ou L’Arbre de feu, depicting one of the weeping willows in his garden at Giverny, sold for €9.7 million ($10.9 million). Two more Monets, La Seine à Vernon, Arbres (1894) and La Maison à Travers les Roses, brought in €4.3 million ($4.8 million) and €2.5 million ($2.9 million), respectively.

The four paintings had an unusual history. All passed from Monet to his son Michel before being acquired by the dealer Katia Granoff and eventually joining the Schlumberger collection. They’d remained in private hands for decades.

Jeanne Schlumberger began collecting seriously in the 1950s, working closely with Granoff at a time when Monet’s late paintings weren’t nearly as fashionable as they are today. In 1958, she appears to have helped finance Granoff’s purchase of works from Michel Monet’s studio, giving the dealer access to paintings that would eventually become some of the artist’s most sought-after.

The collection also included three early paintings by Paul Cézanne, but they never made it to the auction block. Sotheby’s announced Thursday that the works, recently designated French national treasures, had been withdrawn following discussions between the Schlumberger family and the city of Aix-en-Provence, Cézanne’s hometown.

The city now intends to acquire the paintings for the Musée Granet, with support from France’s Ministry of Culture.

There was plenty of action beyond Monet. Pierre Bonnard’s La Cueillette des Prunes, which hadn’t been exhibited since 1956, sold for €2.5 million ($2.9 million), more than three times its €800,000 high estimate and a record for the artist at auction in France.

A work on paper by Gustave Moreau, Rêve d’Orient, brought in €1.4 million ($1.6 million), setting a new auction record for a drawing by the artist. Camille Claudel’s La Valse, a bronze cast from 1905, sold for €832,000 ($935,000), more than double its low estimate.

The auction was a strong start to Sotheby’s Paris sales, which continue Friday with auctions devoted to modern art and Surrealism.

All reported sale prices include buyer’s premium.

item.title: Meet the Painter Adorning Phoebe Bridgers’s Guitars - Hyperallergic
item.description:
On an average day in December 2022, the Pasadena-based surrealist classicist painter John Griswold got an Instagram DM from musician Phoebe Bridgers. 

“I remember she said ‘big fan,’” Griswold told Hyperallergic, “and I thought that was pretty funny, given the fact that, to quote a common epithet of hers, she’s ‘Phoebe Fucking Bridgers.’” 

The indie darling went on to ask Griswold if he had ever painted on a guitar, and from there a collaborative artistic relationship was born. Griswold, known for his intimate tableaux and animated collages that evoke Renaissance and Baroque iconographies, has now painted multiple instruments for Bridgers, including another guitar she has been taking on tour as well as a lyric book, a vinyl cover, and a secret puzzle for her much-anticipated third solo album, Lost Weekend. 

The world saw Griswold’s most personal commission for Bridgers, a custom-painted vintage Gibson guitar, for the first time when the singer performed on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon earlier this year. The small oil paintings jump off the aged black surface, echoing Bridgers’s ice-blonde hair sparkling against her black wardrobe. 

The two artists, though fluent in different mediums, spoke the same creative language and worked hand in hand over the course of four years to finalize a vision for the guitar. Neither artist wanted to change the instrument's surface or alter its visible wear. Griswold used oil paints mixed with an alkyd medium to create the images, and the final product is a guitar that is completely personal to Bridgers.

item.title: Wangari Mathenge’s Vibrant Paintings Tap into Kenya’s Paradigm Shift in the 1960s - Colossal
item.description:
In 1963, following nearly 70 years of British colonial rule, Kenya declared independence. The nation was not alone on the African continent; in the 1960s, Gambia, Guyana, Malawi, Nigeria, and others freed themselves from Britain’s control in a watershed period of democratic redevelopment and socio-cultural shifts. Wangari Mathenge, who was born in Nairobi, looks to the not-so-distant past in an ongoing series of vivid oil paintings.

Many of the works shown here are part of the artist’s current solo exhibition, Re-membering at Lévy Gorvy Dayan. Inspired in part by scholar Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s 2009 book Something Torn and New: An African Renaissance, Mathenge examines her own cultural identity through the lens of Kenya in the first half of the 20th century. Something Torn and New focuses on the long-lasting impacts of colonialism and slavery in Africa.

The artist’s recent work depicts herself as all of the women, who each interact in domestic spaces. Toys, books, maps, and the occasional uncanny scenario, such as the green ladder in the wall of “Re-membering XI (To Leave This Steady Unendurable Land),” nod to a period of significant change in Africa. The figures often play with or alter the items in front of them, such as documenting a transatlantic vessel or jostling a teddy bear in an activity that blurs gutting and mending.

Sometimes, Mathenge’s protagonists meet the viewer’s gaze directly, almost confrontationally, while in other settings, she or he relaxes amid an array of items. Through the lens of cultural memory, the artist gathers symbols of resistance and healing. The compositions are sometimes paradoxical in their depictions of toys and nostalgic items with an underlying tension, like “Re-membering XIII (May the Wind Be Always at Your Back)” in which one of the figures readies an arrow in a bow.

“Re-membering signifies not merely the act of recall, but the active gathering and reassembly of what has been fragmented: cultural memory, inherited forms, histories, and ways of seeing,” the artist says in a statement. The exhibition continues through October 24 in New York. See more on Mathenge’s Instagram.
