item.title: The MIT Professors Bedazzling Security Cameras to Highlight Campus Surveillance - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Tenured faculty members at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are decorating the university's surveillance cameras with googly eyes, rhinestones, and glitzy decorations to protest its investment in what they call "Big Brother technology."

Faculty members Catherine D'Ignazio, Marah Gubar, Tanalís Padilla, Dwai Banerjee, and Karrie Karahalios began decorating the cameras in August, four months after the student newspaper, The Tech, reported that MIT would be spending over $3 million on more than 500 surveillance cameras from 2025 to 2026. According to the report, the cameras can be activated to identify faces and objects with AI, and are stationed in exterior locations and academic facilities, among other high-traffic areas around campus.

"We have these little buckets of gems and tinsel, and create these little Gumby-type creatures with googly eyes," D'Ignazio told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. None of the adornments interfere with the camera function, but are intended to remind passersby that they are under surveillance.

In a faculty newsletter announcing the deliberately unwieldy project name, "The Initiative to Beautify the AI-capable Surveillance Benevolently Installed by our Administrator Overseers and the MIT Corporation In Collaboration with Big Brother Tech Companies," the faculty members said that the campus had been transformed into an "AI-capable Panopticon."

"Many of us would not feel safer with cameras on all around us, especially not ones with AI," Gubar told Hyperallergic over the phone. While the university established a faculty advisory committee to determine whether the cameras should utilize AI technology, many eligible members were barred from participating, as first reported by local outlet Cambridge Day.

"They knew where we were coming from and what our viewpoint on the committee would be," D'Ignazio added. "Our viewpoint isn't just a matter of opinion. It's grounded in scholarly expertise. I've worked on how data, surveillance, and technology particularly affects women and marginalized groups."

An MIT spokesperson told Hyperallergic that the new cameras are "intended to close gaps in MIT’s existing security camera coverage."

Faculty took inspiration from artist and MIT alumnus Jill Magid, who rhinestoned CCTV cameras at Amsterdam's police headquarters in 2002.

"I wanted to question the visible and invisible parts of surveillance," Magid told Hyperallergic. After Amsterdam police initially turned down the artist's request to bedazzle the cameras, Magid created her own temporary fictitious company, System Azure Security Ornamentation, and successfully got herself a paid job. She advertised her business on silk screen posters that read "Big Brother in Drag," and when the larger police system shut down her enterprise, she distributed flyers urging, "Bring Back the Glam."

Faculty printed out several of Magid's posters and distributed them to students, faculty, and staff, many of whom have joined in on the seven decoration sessions so far.

While MIT Police usually only intervene by removing the decorations after the sessions, Gubar allegedly had to give her name to a suspicious officer on one occasion.

"I wasn't going to let a student or staff member give their name," said Gubar, who clarified that her tenured status protects her from severe administrative pushback.

The professor has noticed that most other participants, especially students, are hesitant to speak out about the surveillance cameras or disclose their names for fear of retaliation, an anxiety confirmed by other universities' tactics and actions. During the 2023-4 academic year, Columbia University's surveillance cameras helped administrators identify and punish pro-Palestine student protesters. In May 2026, a pro-Palestine student filed a federal lawsuit against the University of Michigan for surveilling and harassing him over his advocacy.

"The goal should be for all of us to be able to protest against surveillance, whether that be students or staff," Gubar added. "It shouldn't just be a privilege for tenured faculty."

item.title: Revisit Claes Oldenburg’s Seminal ‘Six Themes’ 50 Years After Its Debut - Colossal
item.description:
Claes Oldenburg’s (1929-2022) most famous piece of writing is his statement titled “I Am For…” which graced an exhibition catalogue in 1961 and starts:

I am for an art that is political-erotical-mystical, that does something other than sit on its ass in a museum. / I am for an art that grows up not knowing it is art at all, an art given the chance of having a starting point of zero. / I am for an art that embroils itself with the everyday crap and still comes out on top. / I am for an art that imitates the human, that is comic, if necessary, or violent, or whatever is necessary. / I am for all art that takes its form from the lines of life itself, that twists and extends and accumulates and spits and drips, and is heavy and coarse and blunt and sweet and stupid as life itself.

In all, the statement runs about 700 words. The piece is worth reading all the way through, especially for anyone stuck at a creative impasse, as Oldenburg later described it as a “slightly satirical ode or paean to the possibilities of using anything in one’s surroundings (mostly urban) as a starting point for art.” “I Am For…” is often described as a manifesto, although the artist insisted it was not. I happen to have the last line quoted above tattooed on my arm anyway.

Claes Oldenburg’s large-scale installations are iconic, typically taking everyday items and tools and ramping them up to a monumental size. Perhaps the most famous, “Spoonbridge and Cherry” (1988), was made in collaboration with his wife and fellow artist Coosje van Bruggen and has pride of place over a pond in the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden. At the entrance of the Denver Art Museum, “Big Sweep” (2006) depicts a broom whisking crumpled paper into a dust pan. And in the Sculpture Garden of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., “Typewriter Eraser, Scale X” (1998-99) depicts a giant vintage eraser with a small attached brush used to manually edit typewritten texts.

The latter motif is also one of Oldenburg’s “Six Themes,” explored in-depth from the 1970s onward. These subjects, which spurred myriad artworks apiece, consist of Geometric Mouse, Three-Way Plug, Fagends, Clothespin, Typewriter Eraser, and Standing Mitt with Ball. Sketches and material explorations prompted numerous interpretations of these seemingly mundane objects.

Oldenburg scaled up the clothespin, for example, so it stood like a giant figure, and he also produced soft prototypes made of stuffed, sewn canvas. He said that “a requirement of any subject is that it be extremely adaptable, especially in scale, so that a small clothespin would be as interesting as a clothespin a hundred feet high.”

The artist was also sensitive to objects’ potential for dynamism where we might not expect it. In “Typewriter Eraser, Scale X,” the round rubber wheel appears to careen across the lawn, its bristles getting blown back in the wind. (The first time I saw one of the Typewriter Eraser works, I thought it was meant to be a wheel that had absconded from its vehicle.)

Oldenburg privileged re-creating objects rather than utilizing found examples, so although they have a readymade-like quality, they’re anything but. He studied his source material from every angle, working with a team to fabricate giant installations that retain the familiarity of the original but challenge viewers to see them afresh. Over time, as some of the original objects have become obsolete—namely the typewriter eraser and the movie film projector, the profile view of which inspired the Geometric Mouse works—they’ve assumed an unintentional abstraction.

Several sculptures from the series go on view next month at Paula Cooper Gallery in the aptly titled Six Themes, which in turn takes its name from the landmark survey exhibition staged at the Walker Art Center in 1975. Afterward, the show traveled to the Denver Art Museum, Seattle Art Museum, New Orleans Museum of Art, and the Art Gallery of Ontario, Toronto.

The new Six Themes is an ode to Oldenburg’s seminal pieces that have not been celebrated collectively since they were first shown 50 years ago. The exhibition includes significant works representing each of the half dozen subjects, including rarely seen examples from the artist’s estate and private collections. The show opens on November 5 and continues through December 19 in New York.

item.title: In Rare Market Moment, Hilma af Klint Painting Comes to Auction in Sweden - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A Swedish auction house will sell an abstract painting by Hilma af Klint, an artist whose work almost never comes to market.

The painting, titled Ser III No. 5 (1920), will be sold by the Stockholm-based Bukowskis house during a November 19 sale of modern art and design objects. It has been given an estimate of $600,000–$800,000, and if it reaches even its low estimate, the work will shatter af Klint’s prior auction record.

Once a relatively obscure figure within 20th-century art history, af Klint has come to be seen as a giant of her time. A hit 2018 Guggenheim Museum retrospective in New York credited her with inventing abstraction.

The Swedish artist’s paintings, often composed of pyramids, looping lines, and flowerlike forms, were inspired by her encounters with spirits from worlds beyond our own. Her spiritualism led her to conceptualize a temple to house her work that was never realized. Her great-grandnephew, who also chairs her foundation, has sought to realize that temple, which would act as a repository for her art and keep it out of museums, but no such plan to open the structure has materialized yet.

Though af Klint’s work is increasingly being shown in art museums, with the Grand Palais having mounted a survey in Paris earlier this year, it’s unusual to see her work pop up in commercial galleries and on the auction block. So rare are market opportunities that anytime one does happen, it’s considered an event. When David Zwirner gallery exhibited her “Tree of Knowledge” series in 2021, the work was promptly bought by Glenstone, a museum in Potomac, Maryland, founded by Mitchell Rales and Emily Wei Rales.

Af Klint’s foundation has sought to tightly control how her work is shown, which is why it is rarely made available for sale. According to the foundation, af Klint herself demanded that her art not be commercialized. A plan to forge a potential relationship between the foundation and David Zwirner fell through after two of af Klint’s descendants inveighed against it. (The family’s controversial stewardship of af Klint’s legacy has reportedly generated disagreement behind the scenes at the foundation.)

Bukowskis said that Ser III No. 5, one of 85 paintings af Klint produced during a three-month burst of artistic activity in 1920, had been held by the same unidentified collector since 1995. The collector purchased the work after the foundation made “a small number of works” available for sale in the early ’90s, the house stated in its release.

According to Bukowskis, only two of af Klint’s paintings have ever been sold at auction, “both more than 30 years ago.”

It was not clear to what degree, if at all, the Hilma af Klint Foundation was involved in the plan to sell Ser III No. 5. ARTnews has reached out to the foundation for comment.

item.title: Collector Libbie Mugrabi Faces New Legal Battle Over 1982 Basquiat to Satisfy $2.3 M. Judgment - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Earlier this month, the real estate company 320 E 82nd Owner, LLC filed a petition seeking to compel socialite art collector Libbie Mugrabi and the auction house Phillips to turn over an untitled 1982 Jean-Michel Basquiat painting in the latter’s possession in order to satisfy a $2.3 million judgment.

New York County Supreme Court judge Linda M. Capitti pushed the petition forward last week, approving an order on October 14 preventing the sale or transfer of the Basquiat and compelling Mugrabi and Phillips to appear in court on November 17 to show cause for why the Basquiat—as well as Mugrabi’s 100 percent membership interest in Moo Moo Enterprises, Inc., which holds the work—should not be turned over to satisfy the debt. Mugrabi has yet to respond to the petition or the judge’s order.

The $2.3 million judgment stems from rent Mugrabi failed to pay to 320 E 82nd Owner, LLC while living at the Park Mansion, a Beaux-Arts building in Yorkville, between 2019 and 2020. Mugrabi was ordered by a Manhattan court in 2023 to pay $1.8 million in back rent and attorney’s fees. After an inquest in June, a judge agreed to add 9 percent statutory interest, bringing the total to $2.3 million.

The Basquiat painting has been in Phillips’s possession since at least October 2024, when it was consigned to the house for a sale in London. However, the auction house pulled the painting from the sale after a lien dispute surfaced.

According to Mugrabi’s own complaint in a related case, financiers Ian Peck and Terence Doran, the directors of the art-lending firm Art Capital Group, LLC and of a related entity, Empire Chesapeake Holdings, LLC, claimed an interest in the work tied to a $3 million loan arrangement. Mugrabi has disputed that the lien was ever valid, claiming that the Basquiat was pledged as collateral in an October 2023 term sheet, but was substituted with the 1964 Andy Warhol work Jackie the following month. Mugrabi also said the $3 million loan was never completed.

In July, a judge granted Mugrabi partial summary judgment in that dispute, finding that Peck and Doran had no right to maintain their lien on the Basquiat because the loan was never funded and any owed fees were covered by their sale of the Warhol. Peck and Doran have appealed that ruling.

Mugrabi has claimed that the painting is worth more than $30 million. In the petition filed by Goetz Platzer LLP, on behalf of 320 East 82nd Owner, LLC, the value of the painting is pegged at $4 million–$6 million.

The petition is the latest in a long line of legal headaches for Mugrabi since her acrimonious divorce from billionaire art collector David Mugrabi in 2018. In addition to the Art Capital Group and 320 E 82nd Owner disputes, both ongoing, Mugrabi was ordered in September to sell her mansion in Bridgehampton, New York, after failing to make payments toward a $3.5 million mortgage. The property sold at the court-ordered auction for $5.86 million, far short of the $25 million she said it was worth, and Mugrabi has said she is moving to Florida.

In seeking the freeze of the Basquiat on an emergency basis, the landlord’s attorneys pointed to a September 25 New York Post article in which, they said, Mugrabi made clear she was leaving New York “presumably with all of her possessions.” This, the attorneys claimed, raised the risk that the Basquiat could be removed from the court’s reach.

Phillips did not respond to a request for comment. Mugrabi could not be reached for comment, as it was not clear who currently represents the socialite after she reportedly fired her attorney, Claude Castro of Castro Law Group, last month.

item.title: 5 Pro Tips For Conserving Your Art Collection - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In the world of contemporary art, the maintenance and conservation of paintings usually takes place in strict confidence. But the discretion that damaged art requires does come at an unintended cost, leaving many collectors in the dark about how to navigate the surprising and complex journeys paintings take through time. When defects can be so readily photoshopped out, it’s even easy to fall prey to the illusion that paint doesn’t age at all.

In truth, paintings have always been needier and more mutable than they seem. If you know where to look, the histories of famous collections are full of stewards: people from all walks of life, from the Medici to Diego Velázquez, who have diligently supported the quiet work necessary to preserve paintings of all kinds, whether they be the holdings of a king, or a handful of beloved canvases inherited from a parent.

Living with art has its twists and turns, but with the right mindset and tools, these need not cause anxiety. Stewardship of a collection can become a source of joy and fulfillment. After all, it’s thanks to the choices of art’s caretakers that we understand what we do of art history. The following set of “pro tips” is an invitation to walk down this rewarding path.

item.title: Fondation Louis Vuitton Reunites Hundreds of Masterpieces Once Owned by One France’s Most Important, Though Now Forgotten, Collectors - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Vincent van Gogh’s Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe, January 1889 emerges like a vaguely familiar, climactic apparition about a third of the way through the new blockbuster exhibition at the Fondation Louis Vuitton (FLV) in Paris. Here, we find “poor Vincent,” as he is occasionally referred to in the exhibition catalog, smoking a pipe, an activity he associated with calm contemplation. Behind him, swaths of orange and red form a bold contrast to his green jacket and matching green eyes, which steadily look back at us. As the painting’s title notes, we see the artist with his left ear in a white dressing; the work is one of two self-portraits he made after cutting off his earlobe following a fight with Paul Gauguin.

While van Gogh, painted in his now iconic style, is immediately recognizable, this particular portrait, like so many paintings in this exhibition of modern art icons, feels almost new.

Indeed, few have seen Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe for decades. The last time it was loaned to a public exhibition by its owners, reportedly the Greek shipping billionaire Niarchos family, was in 1990. The van Gogh self-portrait is not the only rare masterpiece to be discovered in “Gustave Fayet, Collector-Designer: Icons of Modern Art,” which is dedicated to resurrecting Fayet, the nearly forgotten, but influential French art collector and designer, who was dazzlingly connected to the French avant-garde at the dawn of the 20th century. He was among a critical handful who helped build their international renown when few others were willing. “[Fayet] was important, because he was one of the first in France to understand van Gogh, Gauguin, and to support Odilon Redon,” exhibition cocurator Sylvie Patry told ARTnews, adding that he was “adventurous in a really positive sense, and had a form of audacity in his choices.”

Since its opening in 2014, the Fondation Louis Vuitton has become known for mounting major surveys for blue-chip artists, from Mark Rothko to Gerhard Richter. Devoting its fall exhibition to a relatively unknown individual and his collection might seem like a risky choice, but “exhibitions on subjects that haven’t been addressed fall squarely within our remit,” FLV artistic director Suzanne Pagé told ARTnews. “Especially when it offers an opportunity to present major works of modernity that have never been shown in France.”

That opportunity was not wasted. The Fondation has managed to gather over 250 artworks that once belonged to Fayet’s collection, rich in Post-Impressionism. Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Pipe is just one of the many treasures that have rarely, if ever, been seen by the wider public that make up this must-see exhibition, spanning the entire museum (on view through March 8).

In addition to regrouping much of his collection, the museum has devoted a few galleries to Fayet’s own artistic creations, which are a delightful discovery that does not compete with the iconic works, from Gauguin’s Yellow Christ (1889) to Paul Cezanne’s The Great Pine (1887–89), hanging elsewhere. Fayet’s own paintings range from naturalist landscapes to more modern, color-rich experiments, their synthesized forms clearly influenced by the artists he collected. Elsewhere are almost psychedelic, floral watercolors in more direct homage to Redon, as well as book illustrations, fabrics, ceramics, and carpets that were a hit in chic Parisian homes of the day. (The carpets unfortunately still appear faded, despite the Fondation’s painstaking restoration efforts.) The entire show culminates in a spectacular chapel-like scenography, featuring color-bursting stained glass by artist Richard Burgsthal that Fayet commissioned for the medieval Fontfroide Abbey in southwest France, which Fayet painstakingly restored and made into his own total artwork.

Another striking example of rarely exhibited art is Odilon Redon’s monumental ensemble of Symbolist paintings, commissioned by Fayet in 1908 for the abbey’s library. Though the medieval landmark is open to visitors, the library, where these three paintings (Day, Night, and Silence) are housed, has not typically been part of regular public tours. The Redon series is all the more fascinating because they seem to combine his earlier body of works known as “Noirs”—dreamlike charcoal drawings, prints, and lithographs, where eyeballs or heads might float into the sky—with his shift into luminous color and even forms of abstraction that use fantastical floral and figurative motifs.

Fayet was a close friend of Redon’s and is thought to have owned over 300 works by him, along with dozens more by Nabis artists. The sheer numbers and names featured in this exhibit speak for themselves. On view are 86 works by Redon, 78 by Gauguin, 10 by van Gogh, and multiple by Cezanne, Edgar Degas, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Berthe Morisot, Paul Signac, Pierre Bonnard, Edouard Vuillard, and Henri Matisse.

During his lifetime, Fayet is thought to have owned about 750 artworks at one point, but his collection was constantly changing, due to the many exchanges and sales he made. This was known to happen when a sizeable chance for resale profit presented itself—though this was more the exception than the rule.

“He made a few nice deals with some Gauguins, but if he was really collecting in order to speculate, he’d have done it more systematically,” said Patry. “Instead, when the opportunity presented itself, he sometimes jumped. He didn’t like losing money and tended to come out even in the end.”

Fayet inherited his fortune from his family of wealthy winegrowers, who also loved art, his father and uncle being amateur painters. He too tried his hand at it, painting in the nature-inspired realist style of the Barbizon School. That perceptive eye would be a critical guide to his collecting, which “gave him a particular sensitivity” toward other artists, said cocurator Angeline Scherf. Fayet eventually developed a deep interest in art that exalted color and drew from nature to inspire the imagination, fantasy and mysticism.

In Paris, he became famous at the turn of the century for his so-called Gauguin museum, which included as many as about 200 works across all mediums, as well as for his room of van Goghs. At the time, few others were exhibiting or buying these two artists, so to see their work, one typically had to visit private collections like Fayet’s. To that end, illustrious visitors to his multiple, lavish homes included artists Pierre Bonnard, Maurice Denis, André Lhote, Henri Matisse, Pablo Picasso, and Édouard Vuillard; writers Edith Wharton, André Suarès, and Colette; and collectors Sergei Shchukin and the Morozov brothers. (The more well-known Shchukin and Morozov collections have also been the subjects of FLV exhibitions.)

The prescience of Fayet’s vision as a collector takes a deeper turn on the floor dedicated to Gauguin, on the scale of a small survey. Here, the Fondation has reunited three connected paintings about Christ: Self-Portrait with the Yellow Christ (1890–91), Le Calvaire Breton (1889), The Yellow Christ (1889), the latter, considered a manifesto on Synthetism. They have never been exhibited together in France before. Later come Gauguin’s Tahitian works, in which he “sought to penetrate what he called the ‘Māori soul,’ [though] Gauguin himself was part of the colonial world he denounced,” per a wall label, which describes him as living “with underage vahines,” or local girls. It is the furthest the show goes in addressing the controversial aspect of Gauguin’s oeuvre. The text adds that he was “one of the first European artists to view Polynesian forms and culture in aesthetic rather than ethnographic terms, as equal to European traditions.”

Fayet, however, wasn’t an entirely original, taste-defining thinker for his time. He relied on the advice and cultivated opinions of his closest friends, who were often exceptional themselves, a quality Fayet appears skilled at identifying. Artists like George Daniel de Monfreid and Emile Schuffenecker were crucial in turning Fayet’s attention toward Gauguin and van Gogh, respectively. His childhood friend, the art critic and collector Maurice Fabre, was perhaps most pivotal in introducing Fayet to the art world, as well as helping him form his own taste. The two did have their disagreements, as Fayet wasn’t always as convinced about Cezanne’s prowess. Though he collected Cezanne, and once declared him “as great a painter as Rembrandt,” he resold several of those works, too.

The constant churn of his collection and his relative frugalness with his art purchases—he preferred to buy mid- to lower-priced artworks by less-recognized, living artists—showed Fayet to be as shrewd a collector as he was a businessman in the family company. For how important his collection was, it is surprising to learn that he only ever donated two paintings to the Louvre, both by 19th-century artist Adolphe Monticelli. After he died, Fayet’s family did not work to preserve his legacy, all of which contributed to his eventual near disappearance from art history.

This exhibition certainly rectifies that—and then some, giving a window into how a network of groundbreaking, mostly misunderstood artists became the icons we know today. “The masses in France were completely against this kind of French avant-garde art” at the time, “because the most important artists break the rules,” Pagé said. Fayet seemed to lavish in that norm-breaking, but he also understood the importance of listening to the artists themselves, who were among the greatest revealers of new talent. She added, “It’s first and foremost through other artists, that other [avant-garde] are discovered.”

item.title: Hundreds Protest in Colombia After Far-Right President Removes Works From National Museum - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Hundreds protested at Colombia’s national museum in Bogotá this weekend, days after the country’s far-right government ordered the removal of objects addressing political violence, women’s rights, and LGBTQ+ history — including a rainbow Pride Flag — in a move straight out of the Trumpian playbook.

Inside the museum, images taken by locals showed stripped-down gallery walls bearing the haunting silhouettes of dismantled pamphlets and photographs; at the entrance, rows of police in riot gear stood at the ready to suppress demonstrators with water cannons and stun grenades.

Under the order of President Abelardo De La Espriella, approximately 30 artworks referencing LGBTQ+ and feminist movements, victims of state violence, and the “Acuerdo de Paz,” the 2016 peace negotiations between the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the government, were removed from display at the Museo Nacional de Colombia last week.

De La Espriella said he had instructed Minister of Culture Paola Holguín to ensure that “all those odes to terrorism featuring Pizarro and the other terrorists are removed from public places,” invoking the name of Carlos Pizarro Leongómez, a former guerrilla commander and one of three presidential candidates assassinated in 1990.

Among the withdrawn works were a Humberto Rincón Perfetti photograph from an LGBTQ+ rights march, a Pride Flag that belonged to activist Elizabeth Castillo, and a pamphlet on women's reproductive rights. Also removed were ephemera addressing the assassinations of Pizarro Leongómez and leftist leader Bernardo Jaramillo Ossa of the Patriotic Union Party, as well as a pen made out of a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 agreement with the FARC. Crafted by the Ministry of Education under then-President Juan Manuel Santos, the pen was inscribed with the phrase, “Bullets wrote our past, education will write our future.”

De La Espriella’s directive drew widespread and immediate condemnation from members of Colombia’s arts community. Over the weekend, leaders at six modern art museums across the country penned a joint declaration expressing "deep concern" over the works’ withdrawal and calling on the culture minister to reverse the decision.

“Museums have the responsibility of allowing us to know the complexity of our history, including that which makes us uncomfortable, confronts us, or is difficult for us to acknowledge,” read the statement, signed by the directors of modern art museums in Medellín, Bogotá, Cartagena, Barranquilla, and El Tolima, as well as the Museo El Rayo.

Beatriz López, co-founder and artistic director of Instituto de Visión gallery in Bogotá and New York, denounced the silencing of voices that “long occupied the margins of the official narrative” in a statement shared with Hyperallergic.

“May the objects return to a place where they can recover their voice, and may the museum once again be a space where history is not dictated but researched, shared, and kept open to questioning,” López wrote.

Reached for comment, a representative for the Museo Nacional directed all press inquiries to the Ministry of Culture. The latter referred Hyperallergic to Culture Minister Holguín’s posts on X, in which she states that the museum may not serve as “an instrument of political indoctrination” or “a hub for spreading biased versions of our history.”

Echoing President Donald Trump’s crackdown on the Smithsonian Institution and exhibits that grapple with slavery, civil rights movements, and diversity, most of the objects targeted by De La Espriella’s officials were in a gallery dedicated to Colombian social and political history. Inaugurated in 2019, the “Making Society” gallery examines “processes of coexistence, resistance, and revindication,” according to a museum description.

Other items were displayed in a section devoted to socially engaged printmaking and photography of the 1950s and ’60s. Among the targeted pieces were works by late artists Antonio Caro, known for his subversive interventions into mass-media symbols like the Coca-Cola logo, and Luis Caballero, celebrated for his paintings of the male nude.

De La Espriella, a former criminal defense lawyer, was sworn in this August after defeating leftist senator Iván Cepeda by the narrowest margin in the country’s recent history. He campaigned on a conservative “antiwoke” agenda redolent of the right-wing rhetoric taking hold across Latin America, with El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Argentina’s Javier Milei.

Bogotá-based independent curator Jaime Cerón, who curated the city's 2025 biennial, told Hyperallergic that removing works from the national museum is in line with the administration’s broader attacks on the arts. In September, the Culture Ministry suspended a long-running federal stimulus program for artists and creative workers, drawing backlash.

“The changes the Colombian government has made overall represent a setback for the cultural rights of communities that, throughout history, have been rendered invisible, marginalized, or censored,” Cerón said.

But Cerón also said he believes De La Espriella’s directive will backfire spectacularly. He cited the case of the Medellín mural “Las cuchas tienen razón” (“The mothers were right”), which honored the women searching for their disappeared children after a period of violent paramilitary conflict. When the city’s mayor had the mural whitewashed, artists quickly repainted it, and the titular phrase subsequently spread to walls and fences across the country with unprecedented fervor.

“Acts of censorship have become the most effective way to make what one wants to erase omnipresent and ultra-visible,” Cerón said.

Medellín-based artist Pablo A. Medina shared a similar sentiment.

“This goes beyond a shameless act of censorship,” Medina told Hyperallergic. “It's also an attempt to erase a history and culture that are an undeniable part of this country. But what they don't realize is that what you try to erase only becomes stronger.”

item.title: Beer With a Painter: Melissa Brown - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Melissa Brown has worn cat-eye makeup every day since she was a teenager. I can’t help but associate it with her paintings, where the sacred and profane converge amid mirrored surfaces, shop windows, psychics’ tables, and bedroom altars. The cat-eye flick is dramatic and powerful, dating back to ancient Egypt, where women wore mineral liner for its health properties and as protection against the evil eye. 

To connote the layering of our daily experience, Brown collages a spectrum of techniques: photography, plein-air painting, CMYK printing, airbrush, and stencil. Sometimes her paintings come with QR codes that send the viewer to an animation. Her painting “Commute” (2020) shows a hand with long fingers and press-on nails spinning shiny meditation balls in an otherwise empty pandemic-era subway car passing in front of the Brooklyn Bridge, a glowing orb of sunlight visible through the window. A painted strobe effect animates the fingers and the reflective balls — a nod to British Vorticist painter Sybil Andrews. 

Brown’s studio is on the second floor of a building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, with a busy deli in the storefront and a braiding salon upstairs. The experience of visiting is a bit like walking into one of her paintings, where the mundane and the performative elements of beauty rituals collide through glass shop windows. Last month, we met there to talk about her favorite Renaissance painting, the magic of encountering motifs while walking around the city, finding answers in flotsam, and how paintings can manifest experience.

Melissa Brown was born in 1974 in Morristown, New Jersey, and received her BFA in Printmaking from the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) and her MFA in Painting and Printmaking from Yale University. Brown also attended the Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture in 2000. She is currently a professor at Lehman College of the City University of New York and co-curated a two-venue group exhibition, Does This Taste Funny? Humor in Contemporary Art, on view at Lehman College Art Gallery and the Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence College. Brown’s recent solo exhibition, Window Shopping, was presented in New York at Derek Eller Gallery, where she has exhibited since 2017.

Hyperallergic: How did you connect with art as a young person, and what brought you to RISD? 

Melissa Brown: I was born in New Jersey, where all of my family is from, but I grew up near Philadelphia. When my parents first moved from New Jersey to Philadelphia, we had an apartment in Center City, near the Ben Franklin Museum. It had recently been updated for the Bicentennial. There was an infinity mirror room with a lot of neon, and an interactive room with phones that you could pick up and listen to someone from history. There was also a glass harmonica. As a child, I was constantly asking to go there and my mom would take me. I even went through a phase where I wanted to be called “Ben Franklin.” We visited his print shop a million times. It must have had an influence.

When it came time to visit colleges, one of them was RISD. I was seduced by it, and that was the determining factor. I went into their Woods-Gerry Gallery and felt it was where I wanted to be.

item.title: David Reed Went Where Lichtenstein Wouldn’t - Hyperallergic
item.description:
David Reed: Terrible Idea at Rodder is one of the few instances where the artist has shown his paintings and drawings together, in this case, those dated between 2013 and this year. Reed cites artists as disparate as Barnett Newman, Piero della Francesca, and Giovanni Battista Tiepolo as inspirations for his explorations of the interaction of color in opaque forms, layered transparencies, figure-ground interactions, and more. Along with those artists, he also mentions being influenced by everything from something someone said in his studio to an email regarding a painting he was working on. 

In 2010, I spoke to Reed for an interview. In it, he made two statements that came to mind when I saw this exhibition:

My paintings are about process but hide the process. [Milton] Resnick spoke about what he called “studio paintings”.... There are certain paintings that you make for yourself to advance your painting, to find out about painting, to do something different and new. I decided that I only wanted to make “studio paintings”. I love to get a painting back and re-work it. Also it means they’re strangely open in some sense. I almost feel like I never finish anything.
I want to be a bedroom painter. I like to look at my paintings as I’m falling asleep or waking up. I like the idea that other people would see them that way and would connect them to dreams, half-thoughts and musings, not just analytical thought and put them in that space between dreaming and waking. I think that’s when paintings really enter you and become a part of you.

item.title: Prairie, Chicago Gallery That Put Conceptualism Ahead of Commercialism, Closes After Nearly a Decade - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Prairie, a Chicago gallery that helped put a range of cutting-edge artists on the path to success, will close after nine years.

The gallery announced its closure on Friday by revealing that its forthcoming exhibition, a group show called “Retrospective,” would be its final one. “This will be our last show,” the gallery wrote on Instagram.

Founded in 2017 by Tim Mann and Jack Schneider as an artist-run space, the gallery had a name that referred to “the ecosystem that thrived in and around Chicago prior to the region’s colonization and industrialization,” per a description written for a prior edition of Chicago Exhibition Week. It sought to show art in a setting that was “free from the pressures of commercial viability.”

While many galleries have closed in response to the pressures of the art market, Schneider said Prairie’s shuttering had little to do with money.

“We were never a market-oriented space,” Schneider said on Monday. “I think an artist friend of ours, Mira Dayal, recently used the phrase ‘commercially irreverent’ to describe her practice, and I think that pretty perfectly describes our program and approach. We never expected to turn a profit, and we never did. We only ever, through occasional sales, fundraising, and occasional grants, raised just enough money to run the program itself.”

The shuttering had been planned for a year, Mann added, calling the occasion “a nice celebratory moment to close on.”

The gallery had a reputation for pinpointing noteworthy talents during the earliest stages of their careers.

Isabelle Frances McGuire, whose beguiling sculptures of witches struck a chord at the recent Whitney Biennial, had her first solo show ever with Prairie, in 2017. André Magaña, a standout of the 2026 edition of MoMA PS1’s Greater New York quinquennial, had his second-ever one-person exhibition with Prairie, in 2019.

Kira Scerbin, Craig Jun Li, Max Guy, Katz Tepper, ASMA, ektor garcia, and Amina Ross also showed with the gallery.

Mann said that Priairie was founded in his and Schneider’s studio with a tradition of edgy alternative spaces in mind. Drawing influence from Chicago outfits such as New Capital and Queer Thoughts (which later moved to New York and became influential there), Prairie showcased a range of artists whose work might not have fit neatly into the commercial ecosystem. The relatively low cost of rent in Chicago helped, he added.

Schneider said that he and Mann planned to continue their work together. “We want to do curatorial work, just outside the guise of an artist-run space,” he noted.

item.title: Rithika Merchant Summons Ancient Mythology and Mysticism in ‘The Dreaming Realm’ - Colossal
item.description:
In surreal tableaux, mythological creatures interact with flora and fauna within dream-like realms. Insects, stars, metaphysical tendrils, and all-seeing eyes accompany human bodies with the heads of raptors. Rithika Merchant’s strange yet alluring symmetry contains what may be esoteric rituals or communions with the natural world. Each speculative, fable-like narrative taps into our collective anxiety about the environment and hope for healing.

Merchant’s vibrant new body of work centers on hybrid creatures and a sense of the sacred, comprising the Mumbai-based artist’s solo exhibition The Dreaming Realm at Galerie LJ. She harnesses elemental phenomena like the earth, plants, fire, water, and the stars to emphasize both volatility and strength. Amid scenes of floods and eruptions, individuals participate in enigmatic activities or ceremonies exemplifying cooperation and determination.

Merchant incorporates “theoretical, historical, and iconographic references, drawing notably on the notion of empirical experience based on sensory perception, the Greek concept of Kairos to question the subjectivity of time, as well as research on the Beguines of the Middle Ages,” the gallery says. The Beguines were a unique lay community of financially independent Christian women who occasionally practiced mysticism. Some communities in western Europe still exist today.

In The Dreaming Realm, the artist nods to symbols of consciousness and transformation. For example, the luna moth evokes the power of intuition and transitions, while ravens represent wisdom, foresight, and a bridge to other realms. Communality forms a conceptual nucleus of Merchant’s paintings, especially in her ongoing series Interspecies Care, which focuses “on social organization, interdependence, reciprocity between species, and knowledge sharing,” the gallery says.

The Dreaming Realm continues through November 21 in Paris. See more on Merchant’s Instagram.

item.title: Bayeux Tapestry Display to Change Upon Return to Normandy Next Year - ARTnews.com
item.description:
When the Bayeux Tapestry returns to Normandy next summer after its 10-month sojourn to London, the 11th-century textile will be re-presented in a new way that more closely resembles how it currently looks at the British Museum in London.

Previously, reports Le Monde, the 770-pound, 220-foot-long embroidered cloth had been displayed vertically at the Bayeux Museum, which is closed for renovations and scheduled to reopen in October 2027. At the British Museum, however, it has been displayed flat, in a darkened exhibition hall. When it goes back on view in Normandy, it will be reinstalled on a slanted table.

Catherine Pégard, France’s Minister of Culture, posted on X that the tapestry’s presentation was “bound to change” and that rather than being a result of damage incurred during transport to London, the shift has been “underway for a very long time.”

The Bayeux Museum has been considering abandoning the suspension system used to display the tapestry since the 1980s for about a decade, she wrote. “The Tapestry will return under the agreed conditions and will be presented in its full length, on a slanted table, to better preserve it and to offer a better visit. Thus, we will see the Tapestry again in a new museum, with a new presentation. We can only welcome this.”

Tapestry fans in France and beyond have been on high alert since the historic loan agreement was signed in the summer of 2025. When the millennium-old textile arrived in London a year later, in July 2026, France’s general director of heritage and architecture announced that there had been no damage. However, two months later, the New York Times reported that the tapestry’s conservators had in fact discovered “two new small breaks among its millions of threads, both of which were a few millimeters long.”

The Bayeux Tapestry will be on view until July 11, 2027. Tickets are sold out through the end of the year, with the next ticket release taking place on Wednesday.

item.title: Patrick Graham, Cathy Wilkes Win Inaugural Bacon Awards - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Irish artist Patrick Graham and Northern Irish artist Cathy Wilkes are the recipients of the inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish Visual Arts program.

Graham is being awarded the Francis Bacon Lifetime Achievement Award for his contribution to Irish painting and influence on contemporary visual art over more than six decades, while Wilkes is receiving the Francis Bacon Mid-Career Artist Award, nodding to her multihyphenated practice of sculpture, painting, drawing and installation. The €40,000 ($44,800) prize fund is being split, Graham will receive €25,000 and €15,000 for Wilkes.

Both artists will be awarded during Dublin Gallery Weekend 2026, taking place from November 5 through to 8. The award program has been supported by Château La Coste and the law firm Addleshaw Goddard. Graham and Wilkes will be invited to stage solo exhibitions at Château La Coste in Provence, France as part of the award.

In choosing the recipients of the award, an international judging panel was established with Emma Goltz, chair of Studio Voltaire in London; Barbara Dawson, director of Hugh Lane Gallery in Dublin; Brian Cass, head of the Hayward Touring Gallery at the Hayward Gallery; Caoimhín Mac Giolla Léith, writer, critic and educator, and Mary McCarthy, director of Crawford Art Gallery in Cork.

The judging panel praised Graham for the resurgence of figurative painting during the 1980s and that his most powerful work combined “visceral renderings of the mortal body with dispersed fragments of plaintive text – confronting cultural trauma, religious repression and existential angst.” Wilkes’ work was lauded for its “bruised beauty and fragile grace” and the use of “everyday materials” in her practice.

To commemorate the Dublin Gallery Weekend 2026, the podcast Talk Art, hosted by Robert Diament and Russell Tovey, will be recording live from the National Gallery of Ireland on November 7 with Graham to discuss his influence on contemporary Irish painting and his six-decade career.

item.title: Paris Students Block Louvre Entrance, Forcing Closure - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Dozens of students from the École du Louvre, a higher education arts institution in the Louvre Palace in Paris, began blocking the main entrance of the Louvre Museum today, October 19, as nationwide protests over the overcrowded and underresourced conditions of France's education system reach the one-month mark.

The blockade prevented the institution from opening at 9 am as students from the grande école, which is located on the museum grounds but operates independently, played music, held up protest art, and distributed leaflets to passersby that read, "We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world's largest museum." Members of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour trade union also stated that students from the National School of Fine Arts are taking part in the demonstration, according to European outlets. The museum did not open today, and it remains unclear whether it will tomorrow.

The Louvre has not replied to Hyperallergic's immediate request for comment.

What began as a protest at one underdeveloped suburban high school outside Paris over crumbling infrastructure, grueling hours, staffing cuts, and a litany of other issues within the French education system last month has surged into nationwide strikes over the diminished ability to study and work in France.

Separate from the peaceful demonstrations, some individuals began stealing from shops and setting storefronts aflame across Paris and other French cities over the weekend, resulting in violent clashes with the police. Riot police reportedly threw tear gas and launched water cannons at some protesters, and beat others with batons, according to the BBC. Though the French government has not released figures about the total number of protester injuries, according to the French Interior Ministry, nearly 2,400 people were arrested, and about 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured.

"French students and workers are currently fighting their government and its anti-public-services politics," one of the leaflets distributed at the protest reads. "We thank you for your interest in French culture, and for standing with our fight to study, to work, and to live freely in good conditions."

item.title: Rosana Paulino Reads the Archive Against Those Who Made It - Hyperallergic
item.description:
On Monday, October 5, the day after a contentious first round sent Brazil’s presidential election to a runoff, Rosana Paulino sat in the New School’s Arnold and Sheila Aronson Galleries beside a wall hung with her natural-pigment drawings of small figures curled within seeds. Most, she was quick to point out, are studies; only two counted as works. She tears up the drawings that don’t meet her standards — or did, until her studio assistants began hiding the discards for her archive. Paulino is an admitted perfectionist; in her hands, precision is a form of respect.

The first Afro-Brazilian woman to earn a PhD in visual arts in Brazil, Paulino sees the colonial past as an active force in her country’s present, visible above all in the violence, archival and literal, against Black people, especially women. Her solo exhibition ¿História Natural?, organized by the Vera List Center for Art and Politics, is on view through November 1. It centers on its namesake, the 2016 artist’s book that won Paulino the 2025–27 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice, along with its $25,000 award. The book’s pages pair linocut and drypoint with altered prints of photographs made for the Harvard naturalist Louis Agassiz’s 1865–66 expedition to Brazil, collaged and stitched onto paper and fabric. Nothing is incidental; even the lettering is smeared with intention. “This history is dirty,” she said while leafing through its pages.

This year, Brazil’s pavilion at the Venice Biennale, curated by Diane Lima, took its title from Paulino’s 2024 drawings of the same name: Comigo ninguém pode (“No one can beat me”). The phrase suits her: On her nation’s history, she gives little ground. A teacher for many years, Paulino patiently explains rather than defends her positions. She reads the archive against the people who made it. In our conversation below, she asks you to do the same.

This interview has been translated from Portuguese by the author and edited for length and clarity.

Hyperallergic: For ¿História Natural?, you’re working with, and against, the colonizer’s own format: the illustrated naturalist album. European expeditions came to Brazil to picture it, and the images went back to Europe, where they shaped how the country was imagined. What drew you to the form?

Rosana Paulino: The book really is a kind of treatise on how Black people, and Brazil itself, have been represented. As you said, when Brazil was invaded, Europeans came to map the country. First the traveling painters, and later photography. That album format was very common: The country was mapped and the results sent back to Europe. I drew on that format because it produced the first images of Brazil. It’s the reference for this album. And why do it? I think that’s the real question. Because Brazil is a country that has never really looked at itself. Brazil often used those same images, made by Europeans, to represent itself, without looking at them critically. When I was a student, around age 12, those images were everywhere in schoolbooks. They weren’t images Brazilians made to understand what Brazil is. They were images made by foreigners for foreigners, which Brazil brought home without any critique. Until quite recently, when schoolbooks discussed slavery, those were the images of Black people you saw. So the book really grows out of those images.

item.title: In ‘Aeolus,’ DRIFT Suspends Illuminated Glass Rods in a Sculpture of the Wind - Colossal
item.description:
Combining elemental rhythms with human-made materials, DRIFT’s latest sculptural choreography invites visitors to consider their connection to nature in an interactive experience influenced by the planet’s intrinsic processes and systems. “Aeolus” is named for the ancient Greek deity of the wind and comprises an environment characterized by numerous glass rods with tiny lights inside. These are activated by visitors’ movements.

“Like wind itself, the work only fully exists through interaction,” say Lonneke Gordijn and Ralph Nauta, founders of the Amsterdam-based design studio in a statement. “It is both still and in motion, fixed yet constantly changing.” Light and glass were chosen to further represent ephemerality and transitions. Glass can be so light and clear it appears spectral, and light is immaterial like the wind: it may be here one moment and gone the next.

“Aeolus” remains on view through October 25 at Carpenters inside of Ladbroke Hall in London. The studio has also announced the forthcoming DRIFT Museum, an 8,000-square-meter space inside of the Van Gendt Hallen in Amsterdam slated to open in early 2027. Follow updates on DRIFT’s Instagram.

item.title: Diasporican Abstraction: A Cross-Border Cartography of Puerto Rican Abstraction - Hyperallergic
item.description:
What happens when our understanding of Puerto Ricanness is no longer organized around territory? Diasporican Abstraction: Identities Beyond Representation, the new exhibition at the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Puerto Rico (MACPR), invites us to do just that: consider diasporic experiences that converge and intertwine with Puerto Rico beyond its territory. 

Curated by Abdiel D. Segarra Ríos, the exhibition is the conclusion of a decade of research that brings together more than sixty artists from different generations and geographic backgrounds. Their trajectories extend from Puerto Rico to the United States, Canada, Europe, and Australia, intersecting with those of artists from the Caribbean, Central America, and South America. 

The curatorial approach establishes dialogues between works spanning generations that share concerns with color, form, materials as well as territory, ancestrality, corporeality, and the natural and built environment. Rather than constructing a chronology of Puerto Rican abstraction in the diaspora, the exhibition proposes a web of relationships, conceived as ecosystems that unfold across the four galleries it occupies. The exhibition moves beyond the structures and categories through which art history is written and questions the need for strictly Puerto Rican, Caribbean or American narratives about abstraction. It recognizes that experiences of movement and belonging generate their own visual languages, independent of physical presence or allegiance to a country's shared imaginary or visual repertoire. 

Perhaps most importantly, the exhibition seeks to bring visibility to artists and aesthetics marginalized in the construction of Puerto Rican art narratives. It fosters a dialogue between works from the collection of El Museo del Barrio in New York, many presented for the first time in Puerto Rico, and pieces from MAC's Permanent Collection, as well as new commissions. This encounter evokes the promise of return embedded in the diasporic experience while suggesting that Puerto Rico is not singular and has no immutable center, but rather depends on who is looking and from where.

The exhibition features works by Olga Albizu, Candida Álvarez, Rafael Ferrer, Ivelisse Jiménez, Zilia Sánchez, Edra Soto, Gisela Colón, Nayda Collazo-Llorens, Tony Bechara, Awilda Sterling Duprey, Lee Quiñones, and Ángel Otero, alongside those of fifty other artists from different generations and backgrounds. Rather than simply redrawing the geographic map of Puerto Rican artistic production, these artists question the cross-border realities of Puerto Ricanness, using abstraction as a tool to dislocate identity from territory and reconstruct it through multiple forms of belonging.

Diasporican Abstraction: Identities Beyond Representation will be on view at the Museum of Contemporary Art of Puerto Rico from September 26, 2026, through May 2027.

item.title: Come Face-to-Face with the Lion Nebula in the James Webb Space Telescope’s Portrait - Colossal
item.description:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has captured some remarkable phenomena in space, from the Horsehead Nebula to the unbelievable “Pillars of Creation.” Things just got a little bit wilder with brilliant images of the Lion Nebula (NGC 2392) captured by the telescope’s NIRCam (Near Infrared Camera) and MIRI (Mid Infrared Instrument). The shape is formed by the remains of a dying star now at a phase known as a white dwarf, when a very dense stellar core remains as it sheds its outer layers. On NGC 2392, the bright center looks like a little nose.

“The central dying star is so hot that its radiation is ‘cooking’ everything from the inside and producing a bubble of ionized hydrogen gas as it does,” NASA says. “The gas bubble, which is the lion’s ‘face,’ features cavernous shells and rings with tendrils that are expanding and destroying dust upon encounter.” The lion’s “mane” is actually the inside of one of these shells, illuminated by the star’s core.

From the human perspective of time, nebulae such as this one don’t seem to change very quickly. “It’s taken several thousand years for the gas and dust to be shaped in this way, and it continues to change as the star drives away the material,” NASA says. The Lion Nebula is changing rather quickly in astronomical terms, however, and astronomers estimate that it will fully disperse in about 10,000 years. (via Kottke)

item.title: The Buffalo Haunts America - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In Cannupa Hanska Luger’s latest show at Garth Greenan Gallery, an abstracted bison crafted of ironstone clay and sumi ink sits on a burned and blackened 19th-century American dining table; elsewhere, a stack of the animal’s skulls rests on a surface with vintage axes for table legs. Haunting Luger’s monochromatic sculptures, which Hyperallergic’s Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian calls his “strongest work yet,” is the slaughter of the buffalo by European settlers under the violent banner of Westward expansion. “The beauty of the forms seduces you into almost forgetting that destruction, but that visual history is embedded into each element,” writes Vartanian in his review today.

Climate change? What climate change? In Florida, a life-sized statue of right-wing governor Ron DeSantis is melting. Ahead of elections for DeSantis’s successor in November, a climate action group installed the gallium sculpture in front of a crowd of DeSantis supporters in Tallahassee, sending a clear, if rapidly deteriorating, message. Its title? “DENIAL.”

Also, filmmaker and writer Imran Siddiquee on Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s debut feature 9 Temples to Heaven (2026), a contemplative and philosophical film that captures Buddhism’s tensions and contradictions.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Cannupa Hanska Luger’s Truth About America

Two years ago, I encountered the infamous 1892 image of two men with a hill of buffalo skulls at the Baltimore Museum of Art. It was covered by a small wall-mounted curtain designed by Yurok artist Stormi Turner, and it gave the image, still shocking after over a century of circulation, the depth of tragedy that it warranted. Part of the Preoccupied: Indigenizing the Museum exhibition, it was a way of acknowledging the care that such a crime demands, in the same way that human remains are shown in museums today, often with warnings, behind doors you must open, or under covers that you must actively remove to see. Turner’s intervention was a way to honor an animal that many Native American groups and communities lived in symbiotic relationship with for millennia. That image came back to me when I walked into Cannupa Hanska Luger’s newest exhibition, American Traditional, at Garth Greenan Gallery in Soho, where the artist sets aside the participatory, ceramics-heavy projects he’s best known for and arrives at something more declarative — a synthesis of wood, ink, and archive that is his strongest work yet. | Hrag Vartanian
